The U.S. Army wants first dibs on American-produced heavy rare earths, and REalloys ( NASDAQ: ALOY ) has just signed a landmark nonbinding term sheet that could put it at the top of the military's supply chain list.
And the terms are extraordinary. The term sheet proposes a potential 75-year operating lease on approximately 200 acres at Tooele Army Depot in Utah, where REalloys would build and operate a facility processing dysprosium and terbium, two metals China has spent decades monopolizing .
In return, one of the things that the Army wants is the right of first offer on production, giving it an opportunity to secure the materials for American weapons manufacturers before they are offered to other buyers, although it is not obligated to purchase any.
This is the latest development in a relationship that began taking shape in June, when the Army selected REalloys for exclusive negotiations .
Now, the two sides have signed a term sheet spelling out the proposed commercial terms: an initial 50-year lease, a possible 25-year extension, government ownership of the land and a privately financed industrial operation that could help supply the military for generations. The term sheet is non-binding, and the final lease still requires financing and regulatory approvals.
Consider what the Army is proposing here.
Rather than waiting for a domestic rare earth industry to develop on its own, it is making military land available to a private producer and negotiating priority access to the output. The company would carry the cost of construction and operations, while the Army would gain a source of American-processed heavy rare earths, particularly dysprosium and terbium, which at or near the top of Washington’s metals wishlist.
Dysprosium and terbium are used in the high-performance magnets that keep working when temperatures climb inside fighter aircraft, missile systems, and advanced electric motors. Radar, sonar and precision-guided munitions also depend on specialized magnetic materials. The problem is that China controls almost all global processing of dysprosium and terbium, leaving American defense manufacturers exposed to Chinese export licensing decisions.
That dependence became painfully obvious when Beijing introduced export restrictions on seven categories of medium and heavy rare earths in April 2025 . Manufacturers suddenly faced delays, licensing requirements, and uncertainty over materials that had previously moved through established supply chains.
For the Pentagon, the stakes are unusually high.
Retired four-star General Jack Keane, who serves on REalloys' board, put the military consequences plainly in the company's announcement:. "For too long, the United States has depended on adversaries and others for the materials inside its most advanced defense technology and China has made clear it is prepared to use that dependence as leverage. Dysprosium and terbium sit at the center of that vulnerability. Our ability to deter conflict, and to prevail if deterrence fails, depends on producing munitions and weapons systems at scale, and that requires supply chains we control. This term sheet is an important step toward bringing heavy rare earth processing onto a U.S. defense installation. "
The Army's own Dr. Jeff Waksman was equally direct, describing rare earth processing as a national security vulnerability and pointing to China's near-total control of dysprosium and terbium.
The Pentagon has also imposed a deadline. Beginning January 1, 2027, expanded federal sourcing restrictions will apply to covered rare earth magnets and their supply chains. Defense contractors will need compliant sources of materials, processing, and manufacturing.
That creates an opening for companies capable of producing qualified rare earth metals outside China.
REalloys ( NASDAQ: ALOY ) has spent the past two years doing precisely that, securing feedstock, processing capacity, metallization technology, and financing across North America.
The company is already developing rare earth materials in Euclid, Ohio, and has partnered with Canada's Saskatchewan Research Council to expand non-Chinese rare earth processing.
Under that arrangement, REalloys secured rights to approximately 80% of SRC's expanded output, with the upgraded facility targeting annual production capacity of roughly 525 tonnes of NdPr metal, 30 tonnes of dysprosium oxide and 15 tonnes of terbium oxide
Those numbers are important because the rare earth business has a serious problem between the mine and the finished magnet.
Mining rare earths is one thing. Separating them, converting the oxides into metals and producing the alloys used in advanced magnets requires specialized equipment and technical expertise. China dominates those industrial processes, which is why simply opening new Western mines won't eliminate dependence on Chinese suppliers.
REalloys is developing what it says will become the largest heavy rare earth metallization facility outside China , with commissioning currently targeted for the first quarter of 2028.
The company has also secured a 15-year offtake agreement covering 15% of Phase 1 production from Critical Metals' Tanbreez project in Greenland, adding another potential source of rare earth feedstock outside China.
Other non-binding agreements involving Montana, Wyoming, and international partners expand the company's access to raw materials, while its strategic  LOI with JS Link aims to connect rare earth alloy production with permanent magnet manufacturing.
There's also a direct Pentagon relationship beyond Tooele.
In March, the Defense Logistics Agency awarded REalloys a contract to develop modular metallization technology for samarium and gadolinium, two additional metals used in specialized defense applications.
And the company has raised significant money to pursue its plans. REalloys completed an approximately $100 million institutional private placement in June and reported $122.4 million in cash at the end of that month.
Its Saskatchewan expansion and heavy rare earth metallization projects are funded through their planned commissioning stages, according to the company. Tooele remains a separate proposed development requiring its own financing and approvals.
The Army's approach at Tooele deserves attention because it could change how Washington develops domestic sources of critical materials.
Under the proposed arrangement, the government keeps the land. REalloys pays fair-market rent, finances construction, and runs the processing operation. Once production begins, the Army receives a contractual opportunity to buy the materials it needs.
The military would also receive participation rent once commercial operations begin, with the exact methodology to be negotiated in the definitive lease.
That means the Army could help establish domestic production on its own property while leaving construction and operating costs with the private sector.
And this is no ordinary short-term industrial lease.
The proposed initial term is 50 years, with a possible 25-year extension. That's a potential three-quarters of a century for a facility dedicated to materials that American defense manufacturers currently struggle to source outside China.
The proposed right of first offer is equally important. It would give the Army an opportunity to secure production from the facility, although it would not require the military to purchase any material.

articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects buyout bid from activist investor and adopts 'poison pill' plan - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects buyout bid from activist investor and adopts 'poison pill' plan - ABC News

articles.content_orig:
Wendy's on Thursday said it is rejecting a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management.
The group offered $7.35 per share in cash on Oct. 28 to take the struggling burger chain private . In addition to Trian, it included investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.
In February, Wendy's board formed a committee of independent directors to assess any potential bid from Trian in response to a regulatory filing from the firm. The committee found that the proposal "substantially undervalues" Wendy's and does not reflect potential gains from the chain's ongoing turnaround strategy, the company said in a press release Thursday.
"Our confidence rests firmly in [CEO] Bob Wright's proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds," Art Winkleblack, Wendy's board chair and a member of the independent committee, said in a statement.
Trian declined to comment on Wendy's decision.
To stave off a hostile takeover, Wendy's has adopted a shareholder rights plan — or poison pill — with a one-year duration, as of Wednesday, the company said. Wendy's added that the investor group led by Trian rejected an offer from Wendy's for a standstill agreement that would have paused additional share purchases, adding to Wendy's decision to use a poison pill.
The rejection is the latest in the long-running saga between Peltz and the burger chain, which dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago. A Peltz firm has even owned Wendy's before. In 2008, his company Triarc, which also owned Arby's, bought Wendy's in a $2.3 billion deal. It later sold Arby's, turning Wendy's into a stand-alone company again.
In 2024, Wendy's named Peltz as chairman emeritus after he spent 17 years on the company's board. Trian executive Peter May and Peltz's son, Bradley, still sit on Wendy's board.
Wendy's also reported its third-quarter results on Thursday. Its same-store sales declined for the seventh straight quarter. However, its quarterly earnings and revenue topped Wall Street's expectations.
Shares of Wendy's fell less than 1% in morning trading. The takeover offer had lifted the stock, which has lost about 60% of its value over the last three years.
Wendy's is not the only restaurant chain that has found itself in the crosshairs of activist investors. Applebee's owner Dine Brands recently adopted a poison pill to block a takeover bid from investment firms Arkhouse Management and Cobblers Cove Capital.

The selloff came a day after the Dow soared more than 1,500 points.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged about 1,200 points on Thursday, eroding most of the rally from a day earlier when midterm election results propelled the index to its best trading session in more than a year.
The S & P 500 dropped 3.2%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 4.8%, putting the index into correction territory, meaning it has fallen more than 10% from a previous peak last month.
The Dow declined 1,220 points, or 2.2%.
The selloff hammered many artificial intelligence firms as investors appeared to digest risk for the sector posed by newly empowered Democrats, many of whom ran campaigns critical of artificial intelligence data centers.
Nvidia, the chipmaking giant behind many of the semiconductors used in AI products, dropped 7% on Thursday. Rival chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices saw shares fall 12%. SanDisk, another AI hardware firm, plummeted more than 15% in value.
The slide also hit some other major tech firms behind AI development.
Microsoft, which holds a large stake in OpenAI, saw its stock price fall more than 2%. Amazon, which has spent hundreds of billions on its build-out of AI infrastructure, also dropped more than 2%.
The downturn in markets largely reversed blockbuster gains from the previous session.
On Wednesday, the Dow jumped 1,570 points, or 3%, recording its best one-day performance since April 9, 2025, when President Donald Trump announced the suspension of a far-reaching set of reciprocal tariffs.
Even as stocks climbed on Wednesday, Yorkville analyst Dan Ives warned ABC News of potential midterm fallout for the tech sector.
"The Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years," Ives told ABC News in a statement.
Tuesday's midterm elections catapulted Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidates to statewide victories in Republican strongholds like Ohio and Texas, both of which play host to a number of AI data centers.
A strong performance in House contests, meanwhile, appeared to set Democrats on a path toward a comfortable majority in the lower chamber.
OpenAI unveiled a new set of data center policies Thursday for that it called "responsible AI infrastructure" in the aftermath of the election.
The ChatGPT maker said it would abide by fresh commitments, including a vow to pay for all electricity and infrastructure used at its facilities. It also will create a "water plan" for each location as part of an effort to "protect local resources," and will "create opportunities for local workers and businesses" for employment, the AI company said in a blog post .

Shares in technology companies dropped sharply Thursday, compounding recent declines and sparking concerns about the durability of an artificial intelligence boom that has driven much of recent U.S. economic growth.
The tech-focused Nasdaq 100 index dropped as much as 6.2%, before rebounding to trade lower by about 4.5% throughout the late morning.
The S&P 500 also rebounded from earlier losses, but was still down 3.1%, putting it on track for its worst day since April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s global tariffs rocked markets.
The broader Nasdaq Composite, which tracks more than just tech stocks, also entered “correction” territory on Thursday, which is when a stock or index declines at least 10%.
Tech stocks have surged in recent years as excitement about artificial intelligence has fueled billions of dollars in investments in, and by, the companies that make chips and infrastructure necessary for AI’s development and operation.
Since Election Day 2024, the Nasdaq has surged almost 40%.
But questions about whether AI will enable the kind of productivity necessary to generate returns on those investments have grown louder in recent months.
“I don’t think this is an AI bubble bursting,” said Ed Yardeni, longtime market watcher and president of Yardeni Research. “I think it’s an AI bubble losing some air very, very rapidly, and I think that reduces the likelihood that we’ll get a bursting  bubble that has adverse consequences for the economy and broader financial system.”
Also contributing to losses were the commanding Democratic victories across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Numerous Democrats who won races for governor, attorney general and Senate and House seats have pledged to slow or halt the construction of AI data centers.
Texas, Ohio, Michigan and Georgia were of particular concern, because they are all large data center markets.
“Today is the cold shower that I anticipated might occur after a blue-wave situation,” Yardeni said.
Elon Musk’s companies SpaceX and Tesla each slid nearly 10%, largely in response to the midterm results. But the two companies are also engaged in developing AI, and SpaceX has recently emerged as a data center developer.
Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, spent hundreds of millions to help elect Republican midterm candidates. Until Tuesday’s rout, he was seen as one of the largest potential beneficiaries of Republican victories.
Now that voters have so resoundingly rejected the GOP, Musk and his companies face the prospect of tighter regulation and even potential investigations at both the state and federal levels.
The sell-off was triggered by two lackluster earnings reports from major chipmakers, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings, which were released on Wednesday night. Both companies posted results that investors generally viewed as mixed.
The two companies were among the worst performers on the Nasdaq indexes, sliding 12%.
Earnings reports like these have rattled investors in recent months because of the hundreds of billions of dollars that are being poured into the AI sector.
Memory and chip firms SanDisk, Western Digital, AMD, Seagate and Micron were among the S&P 500’s biggest losers, all plunging around around 15%.
Oil prices rebounded from Wednesday’s drop. As of midmorning trading, Brent and U.S. crude oil rose 2%.
U.S. Treasury yields, which have faced some competition from tech giants tapping the bond markets to raise funds for their AI ambitions, were slightly lower.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped more than 1,250 points. The biggest contributor to the Dow’s drop was Nvidia, which sold off by 7%, its largest one-day decline since April 2025.
Nvidia is the most important supplier to any AI firm, but as investors raise questions about returns, the euphoria in the industry is fading. Nvidia’s shares have tanked 15% over the past three months.
Major established cloud computing providers Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft also fell, but less than the overall market declines.
Dow components Cisco and Caterpillar, which are both major suppliers to AI data centers, also dropped around 5%.

Melania Trump hosted delegates from both Ukraine and Russia on Thursday to mark a recent six-day truce in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky that she assisted in negotiating.
The gathering comes amid an intensified push by the US administration to resolve the war triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine in early 2022. Officials from the US, Russia, and Ukraine are slated to hold three-way talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11.
"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said at the event. "We must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people," she added.
Among those present was Kirill Dmitriev, special envoy to Russian President Vladimir Putin, who held discussions with US representatives during his visit, according to two individuals familiar with the matter.
Ukraine was represented at the gathering by lawmaker David Arakhamia and Dmytro Lubinets, who serves as the nation's human rights ombudsman.
This event marked the initial face-to-face interaction between American and Russian officials following Tuesday’s midterm elections, which saw Democrats wrest control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives from Republicans, delivering a setback to President Trump.
When the new Democratic congressional majority assumes power in January, lawmakers are widely anticipated to press for increased assistance to Ukraine while scrutinizing several measures taken by the Republican Trump administration, including sanction relief and a diesel agreement reached with Russia.
In the weeks leading up to the event, Trump had sharpened his public critiques of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Moscow stated it remains hopeful that Trump will persist with his diplomatic efforts regardless of the Republican electoral defeat.
According to the Kremlin, preparations are currently underway for a trilateral meeting involving Putin, Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, set for November 18 to 19.
Dmitriev previously held talks at the White House with Steve Witkoff, Trump's special envoy, in 2025. In contrast, Joe Biden, Trump's predecessor, hosted no Russian officials at the executive mansion.
Dmitriev has played a key role in negotiating the return of American prisoners held in Russia, coordinating the return of Ukrainian children to their families, and supporting humanitarian actions in Oleshky.

articles.title_zh: President of Paraguay resigns amid crisis over bank collapse that left millions unable to access their money
articles.content_orig:
Paraguayan President Santiago Pena resigned on Thursday after calls for his removal swelled following the collapse of digital lender ueno that left millions of customers unable ‌to access their accounts.
“I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” he said in a video recorded address on Thursday.
Pena, an ally of US President Donald Trump, is stepping down after the ⁠opposition called an extraordinary session to begin the process of filing an impeachment motion in Congress, and as protesters demanded his resignation.
Earlier on Thursday Pena lost backing from members of his own conservative party. Vice President Pedro Alliana is set to take office as his replacement.
Lawmakers had accused Pena of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and institutional cover-ups linked to the collapse of ueno, which had grown ‌quickly ⁠from a niche fintech player into a mid-tier bank administering close to $850 million in public funds.
“He is accused of negligence at the very least and complicity in covering up the fact that the bank was insolvent,” said Al Jazeera’s Latin America editor Lucia Newman.
“The congress right now is tying to impeach the president and the vice president, this session is underway,” she added. “As a I speak, there are people outside urging congress not to accept the resignation of the president because they say that they want him tried and impeached.”
Paraguay’s central bank intervened in ueno after determining ⁠that it had breached minimum solvency requirements, setting off a crisis that has left the company’s roughly 3 million customers, in a ⁠country of 6.5 million people, unable to access accounts.
“My greatest wish is that the return of those funds be guaranteed, that the deposit guarantee fund fulfill its purpose, and that ⁠public funds – as well as the resources that belong to all Paraguayans – be protected,” Pena added in his address.
Ueno has made no public statement on the issue.

articles.title_orig: Bomb threats hit multiple flights in Europe for a second time in a week
articles.title_zh: Bomb threats hit multiple flights in Europe for a second time in a week
articles.content_orig:
Flights across Europe were targeted by "hoax" bomb threats on Thursday for the second time this week, disrupting air travel across London, Dublin, and Helsinki, among others.
At least 27 different flights were impacted, according to Reuters , with some forced to land unexpectedly and others escorted by fighter jets.
Aer Lingus, Finnair , Wizz Air and Polish airline LOT confirmed to CNBC that some of their flights were affected.
It comes after seven passenger planes across Europe, two departing from the U.K., were targeted by suspected bomb threats on Tuesday and were described as "malicious hoax threats" by the U.K. government.
Finnair said two of its flights — one from Helsinki to Rome with 144 passengers and 7 crew members and another from Helsinki to Vienna with 177 passengers and six crew members — received "unfounded or hoax" bomb threats on Thursday, with both flights landing safely and customers disembarking the aircraft.
Local authorities in Rome and Vienna inspected the two flights and didn't find anything out of the ordinary.
"Unfortunately, air traffic is sometimes subject to threats, as we have seen this week, when other airlines in Europe have also faced hoax bomb threats," Finnair said in a statement. "Threats are almost always unfounded."
Hungarian budget carrier Wizz Air confirmed to CNBC that its flight from Milan's Malpensa Airport to Bucharest's Otopeni Airport, as well as another flight to Warsaw, were subject to bomb threats on Thursday.
The flight to Bucharest was approaching its final destination and landed safely when the threat was reported at Otopeni, with security checks subsequently clearing the aircraft. Wizz Air's Warsaw flight was diverted.
"This incident comes amid a series of similar bomb threats affecting several airlines across Europe in recent days," Wizz Air told CNBC. "Wizz Air is not the only airline targeted, with other carriers also experiencing threats resulting in flight diversions and security checks."
Irish airline Aer Lingus diverted its Dublin to Rome flight to Normandy on Thursday morning, while Polish airline LOT said two of its flights from Warsaw received security threats. Both were cleared following security inspections, the airlines told CNBC.
Air France's CEO Ben Smith said none of its flights were affected, but the coordinated threats are unprecedented. "It's unfortunate, and we hope it won't give consumers any reason to slow down or reduce their travel plans."
U.S. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Thursday that the incidents appeared to be "false attacks."
He added: "We take safety very seriously, which is why, if you see any issue in the airspace or threats in the airspace, we shut it down...and so, with all of our assets in the U.S. government and our partners over in Europe, we are tracking this together and working together to make sure the American airspace, the American traveler, is safe."
European Union Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism, Apostolos Tzitzikostas cautioned it is "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked," in a post on X . "The EU-level information-sharing mechanism has been activated related to aviation security."

articles.title_orig: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.title_zh: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.content_orig:
Exclusive: pro-democracy activist’s prison letters reveal fascination with AI, brushes with Triads and an appetite for books
Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
F rom inside Hong Kong’s oldest maximum security prison, where he swaps books with Triad gang members and studies law, Joshua Wong writes letters like a man desperate to stay connected to the outside world.
Excerpts from his private prison writings reveal the pro-democracy activist asking friends to take screenshots of social media accounts and put questions to AI chatbots on his behalf.
To one acquaintance, he writes about his prison reading habits. “Some of the old-school triad bosses in here have also lent me books,” he says in the letters to friends, seen exclusively by the Guardian. “They read too. One of them lent me Mario Puzo’s The Godfather (lol).”
The 30-year-old Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s now-squashed democracy movement, has been imprisoned since November 2020.
On Thursday, he was sentenced to 10 years for foreign collusion , his second conviction under the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020. Wong pleaded guilty to the charge in September.
Wong is the only pro-democracy activist to be prosecuted twice under the national security legislation. He had been due to be released in January, before the latest prosecution, and will now serve his two sentences concurrently.
Despite spending his 21st, 25th and 30th birthdays in prison, Wong’s letters – written between August and October – show his resolve and continuing concern about Hong Kong’s future.
“The only thing I worry about is that people will forget Hong Kong, and that amid competition and struggles between great powers, they will forget the countless ordinary, unknown people in different places who have paid a price for their beliefs,” he writes.
In Stanley prison, where young inmates use M&Ms as currency, he spends time exercising, learning to play the guitar and teaching English to other prisoners.
“I was teaching English to a Russian,” he says in one letter. “When he asked me what the word ‘totalitarian’ meant, I simply answered, ‘Putin’ (lol)”.
Books appear to be central to his life. His reading list includes Patriot, the memoir of Russian opposition leader, Alexei Navalny, who died in prison in 2024; biographies of Steve Jobs, Nelson Mandela, Benjamin Franklin; and the memoir of former Citibank trader turned YouTuber and inequality campaigner, Gary Stevenson.
On the day of the US presidential election in November 2024, he watched votes come in while holding a copy of JD Vance’s bestselling memoir, Hillbilly Elegy.
Wong gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests , which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared – with his trademark black-rimmed spectacles – on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.
In 2020, Beijing said its introduction of the national security law was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics said it gave authorities sweeping powers to crack down on free speech and dissent.
Since then, activists and journalists have been arrested, independent newsrooms closed, and much of the city’s political opposition forced into exile . There have been more than 400 arrests under national security legislation, according to Hong Kong’s security bureau.
“Joshua’s case is part of an attempt to control how my generation’s political history is remembered,” says Frances Hui, a childhood friend and pro-democracy activist in exile.
“For years, people around the world could hear him argue, organise, and explain what he thought Hong Kong’s future should be. Now we can barely hear from him at all.”
In his letters, Wong says Mandela inspired him to study law and he has enrolled in an undergraduate company law course.
He says that he has lost weight, but has a strict routine of pull-ups, squats and pushups. He also reads the Bible and recites passages from the book of Joshua and the Corinthians.
Wong’s childhood friends and fellow activists say the Hong Kong they once fought for no longer exists.
“It is hard to say whose side time is on,” says another childhood friend, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal.
Hui says that Hong Kong authorities had waited nearly five years after the alleged crime to prosecute Wong – just before his release.
“By the time he sees freedom, he is most certainly not going to be the young boy we once remembered,” she says.

articles.title_orig: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike
articles.title_zh: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike

• General strike : French riot police have fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon while scuffles have broken out in Nantes and authorities have arrested agitators who vandalized a Rennes hotel. But overall, the roughly 200 demonstrations across France on Thursday – attended by almost 600,000 people – have remained relatively peaceful.
• Widespread disruptions : The strike is organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions. Education, health care, public transportation and other sectors have been impacted with many services closed for the day.
• Europe discontent : Anti-government protests have swept across the continent in recent weeks. In Greece , students and teachers gathered in central Athens on Thursday to stress the importance of free public education and protest the rising housing and food costs affecting students.
Place de la Nation, in eastern Paris, is a historic plaza synonymous with protest. Marches often end here, and we’re used to seeing huge clouds of tear gas as protesters clash with police.
But tonight, it’s quite an unusual and arresting sight to see the square so full after dark. A huge mass of people continue to stand still beneath a monument celebrating the triumph of the French Republic.
The protest in Paris was authorized by city officials to wrap up at 7 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET). But with less than 30 minutes to go, it’s unlikely everyone will be able to disperse quickly.
Although this movement initially began with students protesting the state of the education system, it has morphed into one that includes several other concerns united by a key factor: the poor state of the economy.
Protesters on Thursday said they are anxious about low salaries, which have not kept up with inflation, as well as underresourced public services.
“There is a lot of concern about the future, notably the issues of salaries, public services,” Alice Martinovic, an 18-year-old student participating in the Paris protest, told Reuters.
“I hope in the upcoming elections the candidates will really think about this movement and include the opinions of young people, of students, who are now joined by a lot of other workers.”
Meanwhile, Mehdi Dumontroty, a 45-year-old firefighter also protesting in Paris, told Reuters that “our pay has not kept up with inflation.”
“What happened this summer proves that we were right when we said we needed more resources to deal with the crisis that we faced,” he said, referencing fierce wildfires which swept across southern France amid record-breaking, climate change-fueled heat waves.
Almost 600,000 protesters are on the streets of France today, the country’s interior ministry has just estimated, making Thursday the biggest day of protests since this current wave of unrest began in September.
Earlier today, at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET), the ministry had estimated that 270,000 people were protesting but that number excluded Paris, where a march began this afternoon.
The ministry is expected to release its final figures later today but, as of now, its current estimates indicate that these demonstrations are not quite as big as the 2023 pension reform protests.
French education minister Édouard Geffray has condemned what he said was a “deliberate act of arson” at a school near the city of Toulouse in southern France.
The minister thanked firefighters and law enforcement officials for helping to “limit the damage” cause by the flames.
“This deliberate act of arson could have had tragic consequences for human life. I condemn it in the strongest possible terms and call on everyone to condemn it unequivocally,” he added, while vowing to hold those responsible to account.
Earlier, France’s interior ministry said the blaze started after fireworks were directed at an office hosting the school’s student services.
Authorities in Rennes said they arrested “several dozen” masked individuals who vandalized a hotel, threw objects at police and “violently attacked” union members who were protesting earlier today.
Photos taken by local media show that vandals smashed the hotel’s glass doors and painted graffiti on windows.
Some masked individuals also tried to erect barricades to block some of the city’s roads, lit fires in garbage bins, and threw heavy pétanque balls – used in a popular French game – at police, authorities added.
Despite violent clashes like this, however, the protests today have largely been peaceful even as they have been attended by hundreds of thousands of people.
As today’s march in Paris got underway, the trade unions were in a jubilant mood. Music blared out as the crowd, dominated by left-wing groups, sang and chanted slogans against the government and the far-right.
A police helicopter buzzed above, but in the confines of the avenue we were walking down, there was little sense of the heavy police presence around the protest.
In the distance, the soaring statue of Marianne – the national symbol of France – got smaller and smaller as the march inched its way forward.
The protest route is packed. The movement of the crowd has been brought to a near standstill at points by the sheer quantity of people.
Later, several protesters were seen lying on the ground being treated by street medics, with blood flowing from the head of an older man. A bystander said the man was struck by police, but an officer at the scene said they were unaware of any incident.
At one point, protesters scattered as tear gas was deployed by police, followed by mass cries of “everyone hates the police.”
The mood of the crowd has lost its upbeat feel.
Several of France’s biggest unions, representing everyone from students, teachers and postal workers to doctors, pharmacists and transport workers, have called for a nationwide strike. So, how is that affecting these essential services?
Schools: About 13% of all school staff are participating in the strikes, France’s education ministry estimates, including 16% of all teachers. Around 19% of schools and 18% of colleges across France are affected by the strike.
Universities: About one in three of France’s higher education are “disrupted” because of the strikes and protests, the government told CNN.
Hospitals: Very few public hospital staff – only about 4% of the workforce – are participating in the strike, France’s healthcare ministry told CNN. “No significant disruption to healthcare services has been reported,” the ministry added. Two of France’s main unions representing both public and private healthcare workers had called on them to strike, citing the high cost of living and the deterioriation of public services.
Transport: Four in 10 of today’s scheduled trains have been canceled, though a handful of those cancelations are due to other factors like unavailable equipment, according to tracking website Trayn.
The labor unions that have called today’s demonstrations in France are demanding higher wages and pensions. In particular, the largest of the unions – the CGT – says the minimum wage needs to be increased immediately by 10%.
Last month, the CGT claimed there had been a big increase in the number of professions paying some employees less than the minimum wage. Another union - the CFDT – is demanding a 100 euro increase in the minimum monthly wage, about 7%.
Maud Millier, a CGT official in Lyon, said that the government’s announced minimum wage increase, from November 1, amounts to just €15 for someone earning the minimum wage, which she said was nowhere near enough given rising fuel and food prices.
Employers’ groups have warned that such increases would harm competitiveness and threaten employment.
Other groups involved in the protests have different demands. Students’ groups are demanding an increase of more than $10 billion in the education budget, as well as $1.5 billion investment in school infrastructure and 250,000 additional university places.

articles.title_orig: The AI Selloff Is Getting Worse. Nvidia, Dell and Data Center Stocks Are Plunging Hard. Is It Time to Buy the Dip?
articles.title_zh: The AI Selloff Is Getting Worse. Nvidia, Dell and Data Center Stocks Are Plunging Hard. Is It Time to Buy the Dip?
articles.content_orig:
Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence buildout fell broadly again in Thursday morning trading. On Wednesday, after Democrats swept the midterm elections, data-center builders and power-equipment makers fell as much as 20% or more, and Dell Technologies ( DELL -12.68% ) , optical-networking makers, and other AI hardware names dropped 7% to 10%, even as the S&P 500 rose. Nvidia ( NVDA -7.93% ) slipped about 3% and Arm Holdings ( ARM -12.04% ) about 5%. But Thursday was worse for the biggest names. Nvidia's drop nearly doubled to about 6%, and Arm's to about 10%, and this time the broader market fell too, with the S&P 500 down about 1.5% as of roughly 9:55 a.m. ET. The builders and adjacent stocks hit hardest on Wednesday kept falling, though by less, with data-center cooling stock Modine ( MOD -6.68% ) down 9% after a 21% decline on Wednesday.
Many big names felt quite a bit of damage. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom, fell about 6% to $188.75. Dell, one of the biggest sellers of AI servers, dropped about 9%, erasing about $20 billion in market value, and Arm lost about 10%, another roughly $20 billion. Palantir Technologies ( PLTR -9.55% ) , server and component makers Hewlett Packard Enterprise ( HPE -10.02% ) , and Celestica ( CLS -13.09% ) each fell 7% to 8%. Astera Labs ( ALAB -17.61% ) , which makes chips that connect AI hardware inside data centers, slid about 11%. Meanwhile, builders fell for a second day. Comfort Systems USA ( FIX -10.53% ) , a mechanical and electrical contractor with heavy exposure to AI projects, fell about 9%. Argan ( AGX -9.34% ) lost about 9% and MasTec ( MTZ -7.89% ) about 8%, both pace for their second drop of 7% or more this month. EMCOR ( EME -6.95% ) and Dycom ( DY -9.65% ) were down 6% to 7%. Also hard hit were optical-networking companies, which make the lasers and equipment that move data across fiber lines, including inside AI data centers. Ciena ( CIEN -14.32% ) fell about 11%, wiping out about $4.3 billion in value. Applied Optoelectronics ( AAOI -18.76% ) dropped about 13%, and Coherent ( COHR -13.94% ) and MACOM Technology ( MTSI -16.70% ) fell 9% to 11%. Several companies that got their start in Bitcoin mining now build or rent out data centers for AI customers, and they fell too. Applied Digital ( APLD -15.65% ) , which builds large data centers for AI workloads, fell about 11%. Core Scientific ( CORZ -11.25% ) and Cipher Digital lost roughly 8% to 9%. Meanwhile, Bitcoin itself was down only about 1% through about 10 a.m. ET, signaling that investors weren't selling these stocks over crypto. It wasn't until the broader market started tumbling that Bitcoin also started sliding, down nearly 6% by about 11 a.m. ET.
A big part of the worry is how quickly new data centers can be built, given the blue wave that swept through the Midterm elections. With Democrats now in charge of both chambers, investors are bracing for more oversight of an industry that many governments are already trying to regulate. In Texas, for example, one of the biggest data-center markets, the new governor-elect campaigned on pausing new data-center construction. UBS analysts put a number on the risk: If construction pauses spread, they estimate that nearly a third of the new U.S. data-center capacity expected to come online in 2028 could be delayed or lost. For companies whose growth is contingent on the supply available to meet booming demand, that's a big deal.
Perhaps the clearest example of how jumpy investors are is Viavi Solutions ( VIAV -15.86% ) , which crashed 18% the morning after it reported that quarterly revenue jumped 57% to $469.3 million, raised its outlook, and approved a $500 million stock buyback. The firm clearly delivered strong results, but the massive plunge shows the stock is trading on fear about the whole AI build-out rather than the business in particular. That could mean more pain if political news gets worse. But it can also mean the market is throwing out good companies along with the risky ones.
For most investors, not all at once. The political risk is real but unsettled. Congress doesn't change hands until January, and any state-level pause would still have to be written and passed. Meanwhile, a 6% drop in Nvidia is a much smaller move than the double-digit losses in fiber makers or Wednesday's plunge in builders, a sign that investors are punishing the companies most exposed to new construction the hardest. Some see value already. Asset manager VanEck argues the sell-off has left Bitcoin miners oversold because their access to the power grid is scarce and commands a premium for AI customers looking for places to build. If you believe the AI build-out will keep going, a two-day plunge like this is the kind of moment long-term investors look for. The smarter move is to buy slowly, in pieces, and to favor companies with strong balance sheets and real customer contracts over the most speculative names. Just remember, these are among the most volatile AI stocks in the market right now. And if you'd rather avoid the political risk entirely, there are steadier ways to own tech stocks while Washington sorts this out.

The MDR-3R are a real throwback to the beginning of portable audio. All they’re missing is a Walkman.﻿

Many of my childhood summer afternoons were spent riding around my hometown on my Huffy bike or, in later years, taking the bus into Harvard Square to walk around and hang out at The Garage. My Sony Walkman was always in my jacket pocket, and a pair of headphones were always on my head. For many of those years, they were a pair of Sony MDR-3L2 handed down (or maybe “borrowed”) from my older brother. I wore them constantly — until the cable caught on my handlebars, pulled off my head, and I ran them over with my bike. But now I can relive those days with the release of the Sony MDR-3R wired headphones.
The Sony MDR-3R are remarkably similar to the original. They look identical, with metal extenders that slide into the plastic headband to adjust the fit. The same 23mm drivers use removable foam pads that come in blue and orange (both colors are in the box). The design is also incredibly light — Sony lists them at 38 grams, 2 grams lighter than the MDR-3L2.
There are a few changes. Instead of a 3.5mm connector, the MDR-3R uses USB-C. At 1.2 meters, the cable is also shorter, so it doesn’t catch on as many things (like a Huffy bike), and it has an inline remote with a built-in mic. The foam pads aren’t as scratchy as I remember the original ones being, which, along with the light design, makes them incredibly comfortable to wear for long periods. The MDR-3R also don’t come with a Walkman, like the original did. And Sony’s current line of Walkman digital media players starts at $1,900 (with 3.5mm and 4.4mm analog jacks), so I wouldn’t even consider using a $60 pair of USB-C headphones with them. Maybe we’ll see a retro-styled, cheap Walkman in the future. It would be a fun, if very niche, pairing.
I spent a lot of time listening to the same music I listened to growing up — The Police, Led Zeppelin, Nirvana, Paula Abdul (don’t judge) — and it all sounds pretty good on the MDR-3R. Vocals are clear and never muddy, and there’s a nice openness to the high end. There are some issues, though. An upper midrange peak adds a little too much extra snap to snare drums, which can over-accentuate sampled drums in particular, and the bass response drops off, causing bass lines to sound more plucky and less boomy.
Listening to the MDR-3R in noisy environments isn’t ideal. Their on-ear design doesn’t block ambient noise, so if you’re looking to isolate from the world around you, these headphones ain’t it. While walking around my neighborhood, I found myself increasing the volume to drown out the noise from traffic on the street so I could hear Sting holler, “You don’t have to put on the red light,” the same as I did 40 years ago in suburban Massachusetts.
The mic quality was good while talking in meetings or on calls in my home. People could hear and understand what I was saying without issue. Talking outside caused problems, though. I sounded muffled at times, and also a bit distorted. If I held the microphone up off my chest and closer to my mouth, the quality improved drastically. There was still some distortion, especially as traffic passed, but I was far more intelligible when I held the mic like I was filming an influencer video.
The Sony MDR-3R are far from the only retro-inspired USB-C wired headphones around. The Moondrop Old Fashioned cost less than half the price at $25. The all-metal headband isn’t as comfortable as the Sony’s, though. And while the Old Fashioned have larger 40mm drivers, the bass performance isn’t any better, midrange sounds a bit darker than the MDR-3R, and the high frequencies aren’t as crisp.
All that to say, I like the Sony MDR-3R quite a bit. Is it because of nostalgia? The memories of my (brother’s) old pair are definitely part of it. It also feels refreshing to put on headphones so light. They don’t sound perfect, and I would never use them in every situation, but they scratched an itch I didn’t even know I had. Walking around the neighborhood with them while listening to tunes felt familiar and comforting. For $60, they’re a nice way to remember a simpler time when all that mattered was the music.

articles.title_orig: Marc Lore's Wonder confidentially files for IPO
articles.title_zh: Marc Lore's Wonder confidentially files for IPO
articles.content_orig:
Food startup Wonder has confidentially filed for an initial public offering, the company said Thursday.
Created by serial entrepreneur Marc Lore in 2018, Wonder advertises itself as "the best restaurants from across the country, all in one place," available for delivery and takeout on its vertically integrated app.
Originally envisioned as a new take on food delivery through sprinter vans outfitted with mobile kitchens, Wonder has grown to roughly 170 brick-and-mortar locations throughout the U.S. Its locations serve menu items from more than two dozen "restaurants" across a variety of cuisines, some with branding from celebrity chefs.
Starting Nov. 17, the company plans to introduce more dining options through Wonder Create. Influencers, entrepreneurs and brands can pay $10 a month to start their own restaurant business based out of a Wonder location and earn a portion of the revenue from orders.
Wonder has spent at least $1 billion on acquisitions, such as delivery service Grubhub, meal kit brand Blue Apron and delivery and logistics provider Relay, along with some buzzy restaurant concepts. Wonder has been able to afford such expensive dealmaking thanks to more than $3 billion in venture funding.
Wonder's Series D fundraising round earlier this year raised its pre-money valuation to $9 billion.
With the proceeds from an IPO, Wonder will be able to make more acquisitions and work toward its goal of making food more accessible, Lore told CNBC in September.
But as a public company, Wonder will also likely face investor scrutiny. Weak consumer sentiment has weighed on restaurant stocks recently, plus market volatility has resulted in a shaky IPO market for companies across a range of industries.
Lore previously founded Diapers.com and Jet.com, which he sold to Amazon and Walmart, respectively.

The Great Wealth Transfer is starting to impact the housing market.
A record share of first-time homebuyers are paying for their properties in cash, a sign that more buyers are likely using money they inherited from older generations to help fund their purchases.
Last year, 1 in 10 first-time buyers did an all-cash transaction, according to a new report from the National Association of Realtors, the fourth straight year with an increase, and the largest share since the trade group began collecting data on those transactions in 2003. Among first-time all-cash buyers, 28% reported using an inheritance to help fund their deal, compared with just 9% of first-time buyers who financed.
As home prices hover near all-time highs and mortgage rates stay north of 7% , pricing out many prospective buyers, some portion of those buyers may simply be waiting for an inheritance or other significant help from wealthy baby boomers or members of the Silent Generation.
"It is critical when analyzing first-time buyers to understand there is a growing divide among those who are saving independently and priced out of homeownership, versus those who are waiting on the sidelines but then given a generational transfer of wealth," the report said.
Buyers reliant on wealth transfers look different from those who finance and use their own savings. As modern life expectancy increases, delaying inheritances, first-time all-cash buyers are typically deep into middle age. The median first-time buyer paying all cash is 54 years old, according to the report, significantly older than the median age of 38 for first-time buyers financing their homes.
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title_orig: How Melania Trump Became a Dark Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: How Melania Trump Became a Dark Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Residents who were evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as part of a U.S.-brokered temporary ceasefire crossed into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.
The civilians traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump .
Oleshky is a city in Ukraine's southeastern Kherson region occupied by Russia since the first days of the Ukraine-Russia war . It is one of the most dire humanitarian crises of the conflict.
The ceasefire began at 3 a.m. Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
The estimated 2,000 remaining residents of Oleshky were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
Those who chose to return to Ukraine were taken to the Russian city of Anapa, then flown to Homel in Belarus, from where they proceeded back home.
Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location. The measures are to safeguard those who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect future humanitarian missions, the organizers said.
Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them. Volunteers from organizations including the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders and the World Central Kitchen were also there.
Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father over 2½ years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbors but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realized that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it — that was the last time" they saw him, Pavlyn said.
She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.
Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
Fighting has continued elsewhere during the localized ceasefire.
A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.
Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in the Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.
The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in the Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.

articles.title_orig: AI backlash threatens trillion-dollar data centre boom, say tech leaders
articles.title_zh: AI backlash threatens trillion-dollar data centre boom, say tech leaders
articles.content_orig:
A stunning upset in the Texas governor race and sweeping Democratic victories across the country threaten to curtail the biggest-ever spending boom in US history.
That could disrupt a key growth engine for America’s economy .
Come January, states controlled by Democrats who support expanding or extending AI construction moratoriums will account for 45% of America’s planned data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs. A quarter of America’s planned AI infrastructure buildout is set to take place in Texas alone.
That doesn’t mean half of America’s planned data centers are on hold. Demand for AI is off the charts. Donald Trump is still president, and he’s already waving around his veto hat. And Democratic governors couldn’t stop every data center from being constructed even if they wanted to.
But Tuesday’s election nevertheless represents a paradigm shift that could alter the pace and path of America’s nonstop AI spending spree – an investment boom that has, according to ING economists, accounted for as much as a quarter of total US economic growth this year.
Communities fighting against the buildings that power AI
Those economic benefits are already real, supporting thousands of jobs. And AI has the potential to revolutionize the way we work.
But an AI data center slowdown could come with important silver linings. It could rein in unfettered growth that has contributed to rebounding inflation and led to widespread public antipathy toward the technology and the data centers that house it. It could also curtail some questionable business models that have raised serious skepticism on Wall Street.
Tapping the brakes could ultimately put AI – and the US economy – on a more sustainable path.
AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year, every year, for the foreseeable future, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. As a percentage of America’s gross domestic product, that would outpace every other investment boom in modern US history – including the construction of the railroads.
The outcome of Tuesday’s elections could slow that spending, with vast consequences for the thousands of jobs and massive amounts of economic development that AI supports.
Democrats gained gubernatorial seats in Nevada, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, where candidates campaigned on tightening data center regulations. Proposals from the governors-elect include ending tax breaks, tightening climate and electricity restrictions and allowing local governments to impose their own moratoriums on data center construction.
But Texas is the big kahuna. Wells Fargo estimates that for every 10% reduction in planned Texas data center capacity, Big Tech companies will reduce their AI infrastructure spending by a stunning 1.6% (a lot of money when you’re measuring spending in the trillions of dollars).
State and local politicians have a lot of jurisdiction and sway over that spending: enough to change whether some projects get financed, said Mona Dajani, co-chair of Cooley’s infrastructure, energy and real estate practice.
Hundreds of data center developments that are still awaiting permits, utility service or tax incentives could be particularly exposed, Dajani noted. But even active construction projects could be threatened. Texas law grandfathers in some projects’ permits, protecting them from future changes to local permitting requirements – but that doesn’t resolve state permitting changes or electrical service guarantees that Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa could vacate.
The wait for approvals could add significant costs for AI companies, Dajani said: Interest, equipment commitments and utility expenses will all continue to accrue, even while a project is on ice. At some point, existing projects could stop being financially viable.
If that happens, AI companies – who have already strained to build out data centers fast enough to meet their anticipated demand – may not be able to meet their explosive spending targets.
“This is a rare case where state and local leaders have influence of geopolitical-level import,” said Harry Krejsa, director of studies at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.
Data centers aren’t exclusively a Democratic issue: Americans have displayed bipartisan consensus for putting guardrails around data center buildouts.
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott had already imposed a data center moratorium that Hinojosa campaigned on extending until lawmakers establish stronger AI regulations.
But Trump had railed against any attempts to stymie AI’s growth and spending, citing economic and national security – particularly in the high-stakes race against China. Many Republican politicians who may have otherwise supported AI regulations, including frameworks for data center construction, remained silent.
Still, there’s evidence that the AI buildout could be on an unsustainable path.
The United States had 5,427 data centers at the end of last year, according to Stanford University’s AI Index Report , and AI companies have announced plans for 3,969 new US data centers, according to Aterio , a data center research company. But only about 800 are under construction, and AI experts have raised doubts about the viability of many of the announced projects.
If Tuesday’s election results trigger an investment slowdown, that could trim some of the industry’s fat.
Example A: CoreWeave, a neocloud business that rents out computing capacity, recently projected such extensive losses that its bond yields surged to 15% – the danger zone. That was particularly troubling, because its expected return on investment was only around 9%.
In other words, CoreWeave loses money on every single dollar it spends on expanding its data center capacity.
Deep-pocketed hyperscalers – Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft – don’t have that problem. But their stocks have been slammed in recent weeks as investors grow impatient with what they view as an unsustainable amount of spending that may not return profits for years.
“AI is catching a break here,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US.
Brusuelas expects growth to slow from last quarter’s 3.4% pace to something closer to 2.4% if there is an AI slowdown. That’s still solid long-term growth. And America’s economy is massive and diverse. Investment that otherwise would have gone to data centers can go elsewhere.
“It’s slowing, but it doesn’t mean we’re going to have a recession,” Brusuelas said.
It also presents an opportunity for AI companies to get smart about their future AI data center rollouts – and get put on a more sustainable course.
The helter-skelter approach to data center construction has resulted in significant amounts of money getting flushed down the toilet in unworkable projects – collateral damage from massive competition to be first and biggest. Data centers already face $200 billion in project delays, according to Mike Mathews, global digital infrastructure practice leader at risk adviser Marsh.
A more rational, politically sensitive approach could create longer-term benefits for the communities that host the data centers and for the AI companies themselves.
There’s precedent for that. In the previous decade, the Googles of the world built out data centers for the cloud computing revolution, promoting the fact that they’d be built sustainably with renewable energy – even before it was cost-effective to do that. A similar, community-based approach could provide AI companies with the compute they need and give them the political and social license to operate their data centers for the long haul.
“Like the saying goes: If you want to go fast, you go it alone; if you want to go far you go together,” said Krejsa. “If you squander political license to operate at home, that’ll be a bigger impediment to remaining competitive with China.”

This article was originally published at 1:04 p.m. CST on Wednesday, Nov. 4. It was last updated with additional information at 9:31 a.m. CST on Thursday, Nov. 5.
LINCOLN, Neb. (DTN) -- John Deere announced plans to close two Iowa manufacturing plants in the next few years and move production to other cities, in a news release from the company on Wednesday.
Deere said it will be closing its plant in Ottumwa, Iowa, after moving windrower and round-baler production to Des Moines. In addition, the company said it will end manufacturing at its Hagie plant in Clarion, Iowa, after moving STS sprayer production to Louisiana.
Windrower production plans to move to Des Moines by the end of 2027 and round balers would follow by the end of 2028, according to Deere, followed by the closure of the plant in Ottumwa.
Hagie STS sprayer production is slated to move to Thibodaux, Louisiana, beginning in 2028 with manufacturing ending in Clarion, Iowa, by the end of 2029.
John Deere told DTN the company has more than 300 workers at the Ottumwa plant and more than 200 at the Clarion facility.
When contacted by DTN for additional information, Deere said the specific employment effects will "depend on future business conditions, production volumes and staffing needs."
So, at "normal" production volumes, about 300 positions would be affected by the adjustments, Deere told DTN.
"However, John Deere is currently operating far below normal production volumes due to the downturn in the ag economy," the company said. "Employees will receive timely information as plans are finalized."
The company said it plans to provide transition support for employees at the affected facilities. That may include opportunities for workers to transfer to other plants, retraining assistance, retention offers, relocation assistance, severance benefits and career-transition support, according to Deere.
Just last week, Deere announced it anticipates hiring more than 400 people across its factories and calling back more than 275 employees to its plant in Waterloo, Iowa, according to a Oct. 30, 2026, news release from the company.
"With these callbacks, all employees previously on layoff in Waterloo, the Quad Cities, Ottumwa and Dubuque have been asked to return to work," the company said last week. "Approximately 125 employees remain on layoff in the Des Moines area."
Additionally, the company said in its latest announcement that it plans to move sugar cane harvester production from Louisiana to Catalao, Brazil, in 2029. The Louisiana plant employs between 350 and 400 people, according to information from Louisiana Economic Development. Deere told DTN that the Thibodaux move will not result in any reduced headcount at that plant, as sprayer production will be moving there.
"John Deere expects to continue serving customers without disruption throughout these changes," Deere said on Wednesday.
"The company will manage the transitions carefully with the goal of maintaining product quality, availability and service. At the same time, John Deere recognizes the impact these decisions will have on employees and communities. Throughout the transition, the company will engage with employees, union representatives where applicable, local leaders and community stakeholders, and is committed to identifying the best future use for the Ottumwa and Clarion sites."
Deere also announced plans for 2027 to move small planter production from John Deere Seeding in Moline, Illinois, to the company's facility in Paton, Iowa.
The company said it is "evaluating strategic sourcing opportunities" across its construction and forestry divisions.
"The changes reaffirm Deere's commitment to U.S. manufacturing by aligning production capacity with regional customer demand and advanced manufacturing capabilities," the company said.
"By concentrating investments in modern, high-use facilities, Deere intends to preserve and expand critical U.S. manufacturing capabilities, enhance competitiveness, support American manufacturing jobs and maintain its ability to invest through business cycles while continuing to serve customers well into the future."
In all, John Deere employs more than 12,000 people in Iowa and about 6,500 in Illinois, according to the company.

articles.title_zh: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. midterm elections on November 3 were closely watched around the world as a way to gauge public support for the polarizing administration of Donald Trump. The verdict is in: the opposition Democratic Party won big, taking control of both houses of Congress with majorities Democrats haven’t enjoyed in years. Several states elected Democratic senators and governors for the first time in decades – in some cases, nearly a century .
Officially, of course, China won’t comment on the results of the election. That, as Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters on November 4, is “a domestic affair” of the United States. “China stands ready to continue working with the U.S. to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state,” Mao said.
In a speech delivered on election day, Xie Feng, China’s ambassador to the United States, said , “A confident and composed China is committed to the steady, sound, and sustainable development of China-U.S. relations… China’s policy toward the United States remains consistent and stable.”
The first news readouts from Xinhua, China’s state news agency, were also terse, although the points of information they chose to include were telling. In one early article , for example, Xinhua did not mention the historic nature of Democratic Party wins, but instead quoted Trump’s social media post that “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The short, three-paragraph report also devoted the entire last paragraph to comments from a White House official, who predicted U.S. voters “will suffer from severe buyer’s remorse.”
Xinhua published a much longer analysis on November 4, highlighting four “unexpected” outcomes. This article delved into the massive scale of the Democratic victory, from the size of its new House majority to the flipping of Senate seats in traditionally safe Republican states like Texas, Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina.
Rather than offering perspectives from Chinese analysts, Xinhua’s article extensively cited U.S. media, including this quote from the Wall Street Journal : “Rarely in American politics has a president traded away so much political support so quickly. The losses that Republicans suffered on Tuesday marked one of the most decisive repudiations of a president in modern history.”
Chinese state media had much less to say about the causes of the Republican defeat – again, Beijing’s official line being that this is an “internal affair” of the United States. However, Xinhua did cite the general thesis by U.S. analysts that economic dissatisfaction amid rising prices was the primary culprit. And those rising prices were exacerbated by the Trump administration’s decision to strike Iran. Xinhua published a whole article covering Vice President J.D. Vance’s post-election verdict that the war on Iran had cost the Republicans control of Congress.
One Xinhua report cited Iran’s Speaker of Parliament Mohammad Ghalibaf, who posted on X : “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.”
“What the Chinese public is most concerned about … is the impact of the U.S. midterm election results on the Iran war and Ukraine war,” Mu Chunshan, an independent political analysts based in Beijing, told The Diplomat via email. “They are less focused on the impact on China-U.S. relations. This is because Trump has consistently shown respect to China.”
If Democrats act to restrain Trump’s military operations in Iran, Mu said, it would be align “with China’s long-standing call for a peaceful resolution of the Iran nuclear issue.” He sees the election results as “conducive to China and other countries pushing for a negotiated resolution of the Iran nuclear issue and Strait [of Hormuz] security issues.”
That said, Chinese analysts are well aware of Congress’ limited control over foreign policy. In an pre-election analysis, South China Morning Post cited Zhao Zhijiang , a research assistant at the Beijing-based independent think tank Anbound, as predicting that “Diplomacy may become even more transactional. U.S. policy towards Russia, Iran, Europe and China could swing rapidly between heavy pressuring and partial bargaining.” In other words, China is bracing for impact as a notoriously mercurial leader feels increased political pressure at home.
Diao Daming, an international relations professor at Renmin University in Beijing, told SCMP Trump might become more “legacy-driven” in his pursuit of foreign policy.  “On the other hand, in areas he believes he can control or achieve results quickly, he may also take some risky actions,” Diao said.
With a Trump-Xi summit looming later this month, China will be one of the first to get a feel for how the midterm defeat impacts Trump’s foreign policy style. China is hosting the APEC Leaders’ Meeting from November 18-19, with Trump expected to attend. Beside yet another summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping – the third in 2026 alone – there has been much discussion of other potential sideline meetings, including a possible China-Russia-U.S. trilateral.
China had its own reasons to be skeptical about hosting such a meeting . After the midterm outcomes, which will likely result in increased congressional support for Ukraine, there’s even less reason for Beijing to look positively on the prospects of a Putin-Trump-Xi meeting.
“At the APEC summit, if China, the US and Russia hold a trilateral summit, there is a high probability that the Ukraine war will not be discussed, because the midterm results make it harder for Trump to pressure Ukraine into accepting a ‘land-for-peace’ plan.” Mu said. “For China, discussing this is meaningless. Any peace plan must indeed fully take into account the views of Ukraine and Europe. This should be similar to the views of the new U.S. Congress.”
Also with the APEC summit in mind, Chinese policymakers will want to see if Trump is willing to strike a bargain to secure quick economic gains, given U.S. voter anger over the cost of living. There is also hope that a Democratic Congress would do more to push back on Trump’s use of tariffs – a tool that typically belongs to the legislative branch, not the executive, under the U.S. system of government.
“If the Democrats can restrain Trump’s impulses to China and other countries in the areas of tariffs and trade, that would be better for China-U.S. relations,” Mu said.
But few in China expect a Democratic-majority Congress to look too much different. “Structural contradictions exist in China-U.S. relations, and both the two parties share negative views on China, for example on national security or high-tech competition,” Mu noted. “These will not change in any particular way due to the outcome of the midterms.”
More broadly, Chinese analysts largely took the U.S. election results as evidence for already-held assumptions about a crumbling U.S. political system. Xinhua’s own original reporting , including on-the-street interviews with voters, portrayed a sense of pessimism and despair. Nearly all the quotes were from voters who expressed doubt that anything would change, regardless of who is in power. One sample: “I have no confidence in any politician, and I don’t think they will focus on what is right for us.”
That was a far cry from the palpable sense of optimism emanating from the Democratic Party as the election results rolled in. But it does fit nearly with China’s preferred thesis that the United States is locked into an irreversible decline.
And whatever Beijing may say about the election being the United States’ “domestic affair,” it will not be lost on Chinese leaders that an unpopular war far from home, and its economic consequences, resulted in severe political punishment for the ruling party. That will factor in to China’s ongoing calculations about what the Iran-U.S. war might imply about Americans’ appetite for intervention in a Taiwan crisis.
