articles.title_orig: Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein when they take Senate control
articles.title_zh: Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein when they take Senate control
articles.content_orig:
Senate Democrats are gearing up to investigate JPMorgan Chase 's banking relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein once they take control of Congress early next year.
Democratic staffers on the Senate Finance Committee intend to home in on how high-ranking executives at JPMorgan handled Epstein, a source familiar with the panel's thinking told CNBC on Thursday. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the probe of the nation's biggest bank has not been announced.
The Finance Committee is likely to be chaired beginning in January by Sen. Ron Wyden , an Oregon Democrat who currently is the panel's ranking member. Wyden has made clear he plans to make full use of the subpoena powers that committee majorities wield.
Democratic staffers aim to focus in particular on decisions about Epstein made by Mary Callahan Erdoes, the CEO of JPMorgan's asset and wealth management division, the source said.
JPMorgan declined to comment. The bank has previously said it regrets any association with Epstein but that it did not assist him in committing crimes.
In a 2023 deposition , Erdoes said she was aware as early as 2006 that Epstein was accused of paying cash to have underage girls brought to his home. Epstein had been a client of the bank since 1998.
Epstein became a registered sex offender after pleading guilty in 2008 in Florida to a state criminal charge of procuring an underage girl for prostitution.
JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon in his own, later deposition in 2023, said Erdoes had authority to cut off Epstein as a client. She did not take that step until 2013.
Epstein, a former friend of President Donald Trump , ex-President Bill Clinton and many other high-profile people, died in a jailhouse suicide in August 2019, weeks after being arrested on federal child sex trafficking charges.
A lawyer for the U.S. Virgin Islands told a federal judge in New York in 2023 that JPMorgan "was a full-service bank for Jeffrey Epstein's sex trafficking," and that it waited until after he killed himself to notify the Treasury Department of $1 billion in suspicious transactions related to trafficking by Epstein.
"This was a CYA [cover your a--] reporting after 16 years of all of the monies flowing in his JPMorgan accounts after he was dead," the lawyer, Mimi Liu, said.
JPMorgan has blamed former investment banking chief Jes Staley for concealing or failing to report criminal activity related to Epstein, with whom he had a close relationship.
Staley, who left JPMorgan in 2013 and later became CEO of Barclays before stepping down in 2021, has denied knowledge of Epstein's crimes.
House Oversight Chair James Comer, R-Ky., after a closed-door interview with Staley in July, said that the former executive had encouraged JPMorgan to keep Epstein as a client.
In mid-2023, JPMorgan agreed to a $290 million settlement with victims of Epstein without admitting wrongdoing. That same year, JPMorgan agreed to pay $75 million to settle a separate lawsuit by the U.S. Virgin Islands alleging that the bank facilitated and benefited from the sex trafficking of young women by Epstein.
In August, Wyden released a report accusing top officials at multiple banks of "looking the other way" as Epstein moved hundreds of millions of dollars to finance a yearslong sex trafficking operation.
"The report exposes how top bankers shielded Epstein from federal scrutiny by delaying the reporting of Epstein's suspicious financial activity to the U.S. government, likely in violation of federal anti-money-laundering laws," Wyden's office said in a statement that month.
"It includes new details about the extent of suspicious activity reported by Deutsche Bank after Epstein's death, new details from bank reports filed about suspicious transfers to Epstein through accounts at Bank of America, and names top officials at JPMorgan Chase and other banks who were responsible for reporting Epstein's shady activities to the government but instead protected Epstein in order to gain access to Leon Black and other billionaires."
Black, former CEO of Apollo Global Management, was revealed to have paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice in the years after his 2008 conviction.
In September, Black sued the House oversight panel, seeking to block subpoenas it had issued him for his testimony and for documents related to its Epstein probe.
On Wednesday, Black sued Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to become chair of the Oversight Committee in the next Congress, alleging Garcia defamed him in statements regarding Epstein. The lawsuit focuses on Garcia's claims in a TV interview that Black "is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein's crimes" and "was one of the last people to actually interact" with Epstein before his death, among others.
The Department of Justice's mountain of files related to Epstein became a major focus in late 2025 and early 2026, after Congress passed a bill ordering the DOJ to make those records public.
Trump's name is referenced thousands of times in the files that have been released.
The president has not been charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein, with whom he fell out in the early 2000s.

The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years as it warned that inflation is surging towards 5pc.
Policymakers voted to raise rates to 4pc from 3.75pc on Thursday in the first increase since August 2023.
The Bank blamed the ongoing conflict in the Middle East for triggering another sharp jump in energy prices, with John Healey’s maiden Budget doing little to ease a two-year decline in household incomes.
Threadneedle Street now believes inflation will peak around 5pc by the middle of 2027, even if the economy slows sharply.
However, policymakers said price rises would hit 6pc next summer if the Iran war drags on.
The Bank also laid bare the impact of the conflict on family finances, with Donald Trump’s war pushing up mortgage costs for the average household by £1,500.
The Ofgem energy price cap is now expected to rise by more than £400 to £2,150 in January, with the Chancellor’s £100 Budget handout doing little to mitigate the increase.
Andrew Bailey said growing price pressures from the prolonged war in Iran meant Thursday’s increase was unlikely to be the last.
Other members of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) raised the prospect of another rate rise before Christmas.
One member, Catherine Mann, called for an immediate 0.5 percentage point jump to 4.25pc.

The views of other rate setters also surprised Goldman.
James Moberly, an economist at the Wall Street bank, said: “We had not expected Catherine Mann to support a larger hike, and had anticipated that Alan Taylor and Swati Dhingra would prefer to hold.”
The FTSE 100 in London remains up 0.7pc despite the Bank of England signalling more interest rate rises could be on the way.
However, US tech stocks continued their falls this week in the wake of the midterm elections.
The Nasdaq Composite plunged 1.2pc to 25,427.44 at the open on Wall Street, while the benchmark S&P 500 fell 0.4pc to 7,654.89.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.5pc to 53,595.12 as investors switched out of tech stocks into more traditional sectors, over fears the Democrats would limit expansion of AI companies.
Traders expect too many interest rate rises from the Bank of England over the next year, an investment manager has warned.
April LaRusse, co-head of client portfolio management at BNY Investments, said money markets were anticipating too many further rate rises.
Traders are betting that the Bank will raise rates to 4.75pc by the end of next summer.
She said: “While we believe today’s increase was important in reinforcing the Bank’s inflation-fighting credibility, markets may now be somewhat too aggressive in the scale of further tightening they are pricing.
“Growth continues to benefit from strong business investment, particularly around AI-related infrastructure, but beyond this area we expect the economy to soften through 2027.
“Against that backdrop, the hurdle for further rate increases is likely to rise after the initial few hikes.”
Telegraph readers said inflation feels much more severe than the Bank of England’s forecasts of around 5pc in the early months of next year.

He said the latest rate rise was an “insurance policy” against the risk of inflation rising further and said he did not expect several increases in the future.
But he warned: “The bigger question from today’s decision is whether the next hike comes in December or February.
“There is a clear risk that the MPC could go earlier – this will be something to watch in the coming weeks and will likely be determined by forthcoming inflation outturns as well as developments in the Middle East (with the last 48 hours delivering some good news on energy price expectations).”

“We will inevitably have more information by December because we will get more data releases and so on.

Any further increase in interest rates would come down to “risk judgement”.
He said: “Things have happened in the last 48 hours but the whole situation is so volatile that we really don’t want to put much weight on two days, which frankly haven’t yet been backed by any firm evidence that there is a peace process which is going to lead to something concrete.”

John Healey has been urged to cut benefits and lower taxes after inflation rose to 4pc.

articles.title_orig: Meloni urges ‘disorganized’ EU to speak with one voice on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Meloni urges ‘disorganized’ EU to speak with one voice on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
ROME — The EU is giving the impression of being “all over the place” when it comes to Ukraine, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told European Council President António Costa.
In a letter seen by POLITICO, Meloni said that discussing how the EU can speak with one voice on Ukraine should be added to the agenda of an informal leaders’ meeting in Dublin next week, adding that the issue “can no longer be postponed.”
Meloni pointed out the various formats that have been used to discuss Ukraine, including meetings in Miami and Oslo, and upcoming talks scheduled by the Coalition of the Willing and the European Political Community, plus the phone call that Finland’s Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre made to Russia’s Vladimir Putin. She said the multiple forums were “undermining our credibility in handling one of the most complicated issues our nations are facing.”
While the EU has repeatedly insisted it gets a “seat at the table” at Ukraine peace talks, to  safeguard the region’s interests and bolster Kyiv’s ability to resist a lopsided deal, the bloc has yet to agree on a single leader or institution to spearhead negotiations.
“I’m convinced that we all realize how, by projecting the image of a Europe that’s all over the place, we’re doing nothing but serving the interests of those who want this war to continue,” the Italian prime minister wrote. “And I think this is unacceptable, given that human lives and the future of our security are at stake.”
“Proceeding in a disorganized manner, with initiatives that chase one another and overlap, will not help us — neither with our partners nor with those we must convince to stop this senseless aggression,” she added.
“I am not asking for a seat for Italy in this or that format,” she said.
EU leaders meet in Dublin for an informal European Council on Nov. 13. A meeting of the European Political Community, which involves all EU states plus Ukraine and other allies, takes place the day before.
As the format for talks increasingly coalesces around the E3 — the U.K., France and Germany — alongside the EU, NATO and Ukraine, Italy has found itself sidelined.
Rome was excluded from meetings in Miami in October and Brussels this week, although it did take part in talks in Oslo at the invitation of the Norwegian government. An Italian national security adviser attended a working dinner there, but Italy’s participation came in place of France, rather than as an additional seat at the table.
Over the past year, Italy has emerged as the EU’s most vocal and persistent advocate for appointing a special envoy for Russia-Ukraine peace talks. Meloni first publicly floated the proposal in January, arguing that the bloc needed to “speak with one voice” and engage directly with Moscow.
While other countries, including France, Austria, Czechia and Luxembourg, have also expressed support for the idea, Rome has led the push, with Italian officials repeatedly raising it on the sidelines of EU summits and in discussions among EU ambassadors preparing leaders’ meetings.
Ahead of the latest EU summit in October, Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani seized an opportunity during an exchange with reporters at a European People’s Party pre-summit gathering to renew the call for a special envoy.
Asked whether Costa himself should take on the role, Tajani praised him but insisted that the priority was for Europe to have “a spokesperson who can negotiate” and articulate a “univocal position,” warning that otherwise EU foreign policy would appear weak.

Wendy's board of directors on Thursday unanimously rejected a $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid from a group of investment firms, saying the offer undervalues the restaurant chain and is not in the best interest of shareholders.
"The Independent Committee thoroughly evaluated this Proposal and unanimously concluded that it substantially undervalues Wendy's standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential," Art Winkleblack, chairman of the board, said in a statement, while also expressing confidence in CEO Bob Wright.
The takeover bid was led by asset management firm Trian Partners, founded by activist investor Nelson Peltz, along with Flynn Group LP, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners.
The groups are offering $7.35 per share for Wendy's, whose stock traded at $7.75 before markets opened on Thursday. Wendy's confirmed it received the unsolicited offer last month and said it would create an independent board to review the proposal.
Although it remains profitable, Wendy's has faced slowing revenue growth in recent years, and its stock price has slumped nearly 14% over the last 12 months.
In its latest earnings report on Thursday, Wendy's said that U.S. same-restaurant sales decreased 5.7% in the third quarter, compared with the same period last year. The chain reported $547 million in revenue, down from $549.5 million in the year-ago quarter.
Wendy's is losing traction with customers as inflation and rising beef costs force the burger chain to raise prices, the Associated Press reported last week.
The company has also struggled with operational issues, including staffing, employee training, handling drive-thru orders and marketing, Wright said during a call with Wall Street analysts in August. More broadly, he acknowledged that Wendy's must improve the quality of its food to drive business.
"Wendy's has always been known for quality, fresh, never frozen beef, hamburgers made to order, bacon cooked in our restaurants and fresh produce prepared daily," he said. "But over time, we've drifted away from some of the standards that made Wendy's distinctive. While we've maintained core practices in some areas, we've led cost and efficiency drive decisions that weaken that differentiation."
Other businesses across the fast-food industry are also struggling as inflation weighs on customers' wallets. McDonald's reported on Wednesday that it would offer a new array of affordable options next year to boost sales.

The S&P 500 is headed for a near-flat start Thursday. As of about 8:20 a.m. ET, funds that track the index were up 0.1% before the bell. Under that calm number, the S&P 500 is splitting in two. Hyperscalers and Apple ( NASDAQ:AAPL | AAPL Price Prediction ) are adding to Wednesday’s post-election rally, while chipmakers are falling on concerns that voters just made AI data centers harder to build. The biggest scheduled event of the day is the Federal Reserve’s policy statement at 2 p.m. ET.
On Tuesday, Democrats flipped both the House and Senate. Voters also sided against AI data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, according to CNBC . Investors took that to mean the AI expansion will be slower and more expensive. That outcome helps the companies that already own data centers and hurts the ones selling them chips.
Amazon ( NASDAQ:AMZN ) jumped 8% Wednesday and is up another 2% premarket. Apple rose nearly 7% Wednesday and is adding 1%.
Apple trades near $354. Because the Dow is price-weighted, a stock with a share price that high has extra pull on the index. This is why the Dow leads this morning.
NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) is down 2% premarket, adding to an 18% drop over the past month. Intel ( NASDAQ:INTC ) is off 3% and has lost 51% in a month.
The leveraged Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X ETF ( NYSEARCA:SOXL ) is indicated down 11%. The fund resets every day to deliver triple the chip index’s move, so losses pile up fast when chips keep falling.
While the Dow rises, the Nasdaq-100 proxy is falling. That gap shows money moving away from chip suppliers and toward blue chips and companies that already own AI capacity (we featured seven suppliers behind the data center expansion, from power to cooling, in a free report you can grab here ). Needham analyst Laura Martin summed it up: “Hyperscalers are AI incumbents.” Siebert Financial’s Mark Malek pointed to where the risk lies: “The most vulnerable AI companies are the borrowers, not necessarily the biggest spenders.”
Wall Street’s concerns gauge, the VIX, is almost 21. That puts it in elevated territory, up 3 points from a week earlier. The 10-year Treasury yield is just under 5%, which keeps borrowing costs high for the rate-sensitive small caps in the Russell 2000.
The top of the Fed’s target range is 4% going into today’s announcement. Any hint about future rate cuts will likely move small caps and high-valuation tech the most. Through the session, keep an eye on whether chip stocks steady as investors work out how far state-level limits on data centers can actually reach.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s Election Ended With No Clear Winner. These Parties Are Trying to Form a Coalition.
articles.title_zh: Israel’s Election Ended With No Clear Winner. These Parties Are Trying to Form a Coalition.
articles.content_orig:
A majority of Israeli lawmakers have backed former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to be given the first chance to form the country's next government, as consultations with President Isaac Herzog continued on Thursday.
A total of 67 of the 120 members of the Knesset endorsed the leader of the centrist Yashar party to begin coalition talks, after the Arab-dominated Joint List also threw its support behind him, Israeli media reported.
However, that does not guarantee that Eisenkot, the biggest challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, will be successful in forming a government.
He would likely need the backing of both the Joint List and the separate Ra'am party, which together won 19 seats in last month's election, nearly doubling their previous representation and giving them considerable influence over the formation of the next government.
Finding agreement to achieve a majority could prove a struggle as two of Eisenkot's allies have previously ruled out cooperation with Arab parties.
Israel's political future remains uncertain following the parliamentary elections on October 27 that gave neither of the main blocs - Netanyahu's right-wing camp and Eisenkot's centrist alliance - a majority.
Netanyahu's Likud party won the most seats in the 120-member Knesset, securing 27, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar party with 21.
President Herzog has been holding talks with party representatives since Wednesday evening, with each party given the opportunity to recommend a candidate to be tasked with forming a government.
He is scheduled to meet with representatives from Likud and Yashar on Thursday evening, after which the president will determine the candidate he believes has the best chance of securing a parliamentary majority.
The person does not need to be the leader of the largest party, with Eisenkot expected to be given the first shot after the strong backing he received.
The Joint List said backing Eisenkot had been a difficult decision, in a statement cited by Israeli media.
"Although we are determined to oust Netanyahu, the opposition camp led by Eisenkot has so far failed to show the necessary willingness to engage with Netanyahu's policies and to combat the incitement against Arab citizens," the alliance was quoted as saying by the ynet news site.
Netanyahu's Likud accused the Arab parties of electoral fraud, allegations that have since been rejected by the police and the electoral authority.
In his first video message released since the election on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu again railed against the Arab parties, warning against a government "that is dependent on extremist Islam and Islamist parties."
Netanyahu, who is Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is seeking a seventh term.

articles.title_orig: Ancient discovery from time of Jesus emerges near Jerusalem's Temple Mount
articles.title_zh: Ancient discovery from time of Jesus emerges near Jerusalem's Temple Mount
articles.content_orig:
An ancient Jewish historian may have known people connected to Jesus' crucifixion, according to a scholar's research. Professor and author T.C. Schmidt of Fairfield University told Fox News Digital about newly identified possible connections that could strengthen the historical value of Josephus' account.
Archaeologists have uncovered a remarkably well-preserved 2,000-year-old ritual bathing complex near Jerusalem's Temple Mount that dates back to the time of Jesus. It was likely used by Jewish pilgrims visiting the ancient holy site, with an expert noting the discovery helps highlight the broader significance of baptism.
The excavation, announced earlier this fall, was carried out by archaeologists from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
The discovery was made in the Ophel, an archaeological area immediately south of Jerusalem's Temple Mount, near an ancient entrance known as the Triple Gate.
JESUS' CRUCIFIXION ACCOUNT GETS FRESH LOOK AFTER ANCIENT RING TIED TO PILATE IS REINTERPRETED
The complex was built in the early first century A.D. It features three large ritual baths, a plastered pool and a paved plaza, along with an extensive water system.
Located near the Triple Gate, one of the main entrances to the Temple Mount , the complex likely served pilgrims who underwent ritual purification before visiting the Second Temple, researchers said.
Archaeologists have uncovered a remarkably well-preserved 2,000-year-old ritual bathing complex near Jerusalem's Temple Mount, dating back to the time of Jesus. (Stefano Bianchetti/Corbis via Getty Images; Aubrey Mercado/Hebrew University of Jerusalem)
Officials described one of the baths as "exceptionally well-preserved," noting that it stands nearly 14 feet tall and retains its original vaulted stone ceiling and a shaft that once supplied it with water.
"The preservation of a Second Temple-period structure from floor to ceiling is exceedingly rare in Jerusalem, particularly in such a central and historically significant location," the Hebrew University of Jerusalem said in a statement.
HOLY LAND DISCOVERY REVEALS ANCIENT CHARRED RELICS FROM ONE OF JERUSALEM'S DARKEST CHAPTERS
Excavation directors professor Uzi Leibner and professor Orit Peleg-Barkat described the monumental stone structure devoted entirely to ritual purification as "a truly unparalleled phenomenon."
The archaeologists added, "The complex goes to the heart of our research into the archaeology of Second Temple-period pilgrimage: how the area immediately south of the Temple Mount was designed to accommodate the many pilgrims who came to Jerusalem to visit the Temple, and what activities and rituals took place near its gates."
The 2,000-year-old complex likely accommodated Jewish pilgrims who underwent ritual purification before visiting Jerusalem's Second Temple, according to researchers. (Emil Sadikov/Hebrew University of Jerusalem)
The complex also bears evidence of Jerusalem's destruction by Roman forces in 70 A.D.
Archaeologists found dozens of coins dating to the First Jewish Revolt against Rome on the complex's floors and among the debris.
ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH SECRET CHURCH TIED TO COUNCIL OF NICAEA, CHRISTIANITY'S DEFINING MOMENT
Excavations also revealed an even older public purification facility beneath the complex, including another large ritual bath believed to date to the first century B.C.
The earlier structure suggests the site had been used for ritual purification long before the Roman destruction of Jerusalem.
"Baptism, a ritual that many people think of as exclusively Christian, emerged out of broader ancient Jewish bathing and purification rituals."
While Jesus and his disciples could theoretically have visited the bathing complex, there is no evidence in the New Testament that they did, said Candida Moss, the Edward Cadbury professor of theology at the University of Birmingham.

Moss, who specializes in early Christianity, told Fox News Digital the discovery offers insight into the ancient Jewish purification practices that helped shape Christian baptism .
Between the first century B.C. and the first century A.D., ritual bathing became increasingly popular among Jews in Judea and Galilee, as evidenced by the growing number of immersion facilities built during that period, Moss said.
Archaeologists discovered dozens of ancient coins — two sides are seen above — on the bathing complex's floors and among debris left by Jerusalem's destruction. (Tal Rogovski/Hebrew University of Jerusalem)
She pointed to the Qumran community, associated with the Dead Sea Scrolls , whose residents used ritual baths known as mikva'ot for daily bathing.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
Moss said the broader interest in ritual bathing also helps explain the popularity of John the Baptist and the adoption of baptism by Jesus' followers.
"What it does show is that baptism, a ritual that many people think of as exclusively Christian, emerged out of broader ancient Jewish bathing and purification rituals," Moss said.
"That, in turn, can help explain the popularity of John the Baptist and the use of baptism by Jesus' followers."

The discovery comes amid a series of recent archaeological finds in Israel dating to the time of Jesus.
The discovery sheds light on Jewish ritual purification practices that helped shape the development of Christian baptism, according to theologian Candida Moss. (Emil Sadikov/Hebrew University of Jerusalem; Heritage Art/Heritage Images via Getty Images)
Earlier this fall, Israeli officials announced the recovery of a remarkably intact 2,000-year-old Jewish ritual bath in Kiryat Gat, about 35 miles southwest of Jerusalem.

Around the same time, archaeologists uncovered a 2,000-year-old aqueduct near Jerusalem that once supplied water to the Second Temple complex.

articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
The Motorola Signature 27 —the follow-up to the original Signature we spotted at CES 2026 —offers a tactile, automotive-inspired finish reminiscent of a luxury car’s interior. Under the hood is the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip , making the Signature 27 one of the first phones to hit the road with the agentic AI -focused processor. Revving up its appeal are a massive 7,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, a 200MP periscope telephoto camera, and what Motorola claims is the brightest display in a smartphone. However, getting behind the wheel of this fancy flagship will cost you a pretty penny—160,000 pennies, to be exact.
If there's one thing Motorola does better than other rivals, it's making phones that actually feel interesting to hold. Pantone Coal Smoke has an inky hue and a rugged, woven texture inspired by automotive design, while Pantone Capulet Olive leans more green with a softer, textile-inspired look.
The Signature 27 seems built to take a few hits, thanks to its dual IP68 and IP69 ratings , which mean it's dust-tight and designed to withstand everything from a 30-minute dunk in 5 feet of water to high-pressure, high-temperature washdowns. Plus, it's MIL-STD-810H tested, meaning it's rugged enough to withstand extreme physical stresses. That's on top of the fact that it's got an aerospace-grade aluminum frame combined with Corning Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3 on the exterior, so durability appears to be top-tier on the Signature 27.
The Signature weighs 0.50 pounds, which matches the Google Pixel 11 Pro XL , but it's slightly heavier than the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (0.47 pounds). It measures 6.38 by 3.03 by 0.31 inches, matching the S26 Ultra in thickness but coming in thinner than the Pixel 11 Pro XL.
Motorola boasts that the Signature 27 is a record-setter, delivering the world's brightest smartphone display, peaking at 12,000 nits.
The 6.8-inch, 1,272-by-2,772-pixel resolution display, called Extreme AMOLED Duo, features tandem technology (i.e., two stacked layers) that reportedly delivers up to 34% greater energy efficiency. In other words, this display should be less of a strain on battery life. The Signature 27's screen supports a 120Hz adaptive refresh rate, Dolby Vision, and HDR10+.
Motorola claims that the Signature 27 features its “best camera system yet.” On the rear, you’ll find a 50MP Sony LYTIA L910 main shooter, a 200MP periscope telephoto lens with 100x Super Zoom, and a 50MP ultrawide camera.
However, the star of the show is the first-ever dedicated EVS action sensor on a smartphone. This motion-tracking hardware helps capture fast-moving subjects with greater clarity and precision, working in tandem with the “Action Shot” feature on the Signature 27. The Motorola phone also packs a 50MP front-facing camera, along with support for up to 8K/30fps video capture on the rear.
The Signature 27 features a huge 7,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, reportedly lasting for 66 hours of mixed usage. For video playback, the Signature 27 can survive a claimed 47 hours. The latter best matches our PCMag battery test, so I can't wait to secure a review unit and see if our results match Motorola's figures.
The phone also supports up to 90W wired charging, up to 50W wireless charging, and up to 5W reverse charging.
The Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip helps power the Signature 27’s contextual, personalized, and agentic AI experiences through Google’s Gemini Intelligence . For example, you can ask Gemini to handle real-world tasks, such as requesting an Uber ride or booking a table through OpenTable. Rambler also makes dictation more forgiving, capturing your intended meaning even when you stumble over your words or use filler phrases. And with Create My Widget, you can generate personalized home-screen widgets using conversational prompts.
The processor works alongside Motorola's redesigned ArcticMesh cooling system, which uses a 40% larger vapor chamber to dissipate heat during intensive workloads such as gaming and video recording.
Phone speakers typically take a back seat, but not on the Signature 27. The Motorola phone is the only in-market smartphone that currently features Bang & Olufsen-tuned audio.
The coaxial speakers (i.e., two sound drivers built into one speaker) have two drivers in the bottom speaker: one for bass and another that acts as a tweeter. A second speaker sits at the top of the phone. Motorola claims that the Signature 27’s sound system delivers deep bass, clear vocals, and high fidelity across music, movies, and games.
Are you ready for this? The Signature 27 will set you back a whopping $1,599 and comes with 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage. The Motorola phone, launching with Android 17 , will be available for preorder on Nov. 19 and will hit store shelves on Nov. 26.
I’m PCMag’s Senior Writer for Mobile on the Consumer Electronics team, diving into the latest phones, tablets, Bluetooth speakers, audio devices, and other portable gear. I’ve been covering consumer technology for six years. Before joining PCMag, I contributed my tech expertise to Laptop Magazine, Mashable, Tom’s Guide, Esquire, Good Housekeeping, and more.

After months of anticipation, World of Warcraft: Forever , the reimagined take on the World of Warcraft 's "classic" era, has finally gone live on PC via the Battle.net store .
Normally, whenever a new MMORPG or expansion for one comes out, its launch is usually riddled with server stability problems or log-in queues so long that it will take players hours to log in (like FFXIV: Endwalker's infamous launch , for example).
Very stable launch for World of Warcraft Forever. Huge amount of people spawned in all at once, no lag, mob spawns rapid, good stuff. November 5, 2026
However, World of Warcraft: Forever's launch appears to have gone more smoothly than expected, thanks to its "Megaserver" architecture, which handles more players at once than individual "realm" servers in regular World of Warcraft.
Our own Jez Corden tested World of Warcraft: Forever and described it as a "very stable launch" , which suffered no lag while spawning dozens of players and monsters at once.
At the risk of jinxing things, so far so goodish which is crazy by itself. The team prepared a lot since the wildness of Beta. And this launch was crazier than the insanity we imagined but thankfully the team built plans and contingencies. They are incredible imo. 😲 #WoWForever November 5, 2026
Blizzard's vice president, Holly Longdale, has also made a post on X saying World of Warcraft: Forever's launch is "so far so goodish which is crazy by itself" . Judging by the huge wave of replies to that comment, players seem to agree.
People are calling it the best launch World of Warcraft has ever had, with minimal queue times when logging in that last only a couple of minutes, minimal server lag, and no constant disconnects.
I myself have briefly logged into World of Warcraft: Forever to mess around with it before heading to work and was surprised by how fast I was able to log in (only a few minutes tops) and how smoothly it ran at max settings.
Granted, I haven't visited one of the major player settlements yet, so that will be when I can truly stress test this game's stability. Motorola is patching a hole in its US lineup with a non-folding flagship phone, but the pricing puts this device dangerously close to the company’s expensive tablet-style foldable . The long-rumored Motorola Signature 27 is real, featuring top-of-the-line specs, a super-bright OLED screen, and a ton of cameras. But all this high-end hardware won’t come cheap in the age of AI. Motorola’s new flagship smartphone will run a whopping $1,600 when it arrives later this month.
The Signature 27 is a completely new take on flagship smartphones from Motorola, leaving behind the middling legacy of the Edge series. However, you’ll still immediately clock this as a Motorola device due to its distinctive use of materials and Pantone colors. The phone is metal, ceramic, and glass, but the backs are textured polycarbonate. The device comes in Coal Smoke (black) or Capulet Olive (green) colors. The former has a “tactical weave” finish inspired by automotive design, and the latter is “textile-inspired.”
This device will include the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the most powerful mobile chip Qualcomm offers right now. While some smartphones have flirted with 16GB of memory, that’s less common these days. The Signature 27 will have 12GB like Samsung’s base model flagships. However, there’s not going to be an upgrade option for more. You will, however, get a generous 512GB of storage.
The phone is fairly thin in most places, but it tapers outward near the camera module. It’s easy to see why Moto needed a little more space up there with four image sensors. Note: That’s not four cameras . There are three standard cameras: a 50MP primary, a 50MP ultrawide, and a 200MP 3x optical zoom (100x digital zoom). Joining the cameras is an event-based vision sensor (EVS) to power a feature called Action Shot.
The action sensor measures changes in light at a pixel level, which makes it ideal for tracking moving subjects. Action Shot will turn on automatically when the phone detects a lot of movement in the frame, but you can also activate it manually. Motorola’s cameras have long struggled to capture moving subjects clearly, so it’ll be interesting to see if the EVS fixes that.
If you’ve been thinking about a smaller phone, the Signature 27 isn’t for you. This phone sports a sizable 6.8-inch OLED screen with a 120Hz refresh rate. This is a tandem OLED panel, which uses stacked pixels to increase brightness. Moto claims the Signature 27 can hit an impressive 12,000 nits of peak brightness, which is four times higher than the iPhone 18 Pro Max (and the highest of any smartphone). A possible drawback is that tandem OLEDs tend to have a somewhat uneven appearance at low brightness with solid colors, but we haven’t seen the Signature 27 in person yet to say whether or not that’s the case here.
A display like that could really drain your battery, but the Signature 27 has capacity to spare. The 7,000 mAh silicon-carbon cell is the largest of any mainstream smartphone, 1,000 mAh larger than the Galaxy S26 Ultra . Motorola estimates it could last two days on a charge, and it won’t take long to refill. With a compatible USB-C charger (not included), the Signature 27 can reach speeds up to 90W. Moto claims up to 12 hours of usage in 12 minutes of charging.
The Motorola Signature 27 will ship with Android 17 and Moto’s Hello UI customizations. The company promises seven years of OS updates, on par with Samsung and Google.
This will be a full Gemini Intelligence device, entitling it to Google’s most expansive list of AI features. Moto says the Signature 27 will get Google’s agentic app control, Create My Widget, Sign-to-Text, and Rambler voice input. However, these features will arrive “in the coming months,” as most of those features are still limited to Pixel phones.
Moto is still offering a parallel set of AI features on its phones. Features like Catch me up (notification summaries) and Pay Attention (meeting notes) are still supported, but the company appears to have dropped the Moto AI branding. Instead, these are all part of Motorola Qira, an AI platform that also connects your Motorola phone to Lenovo computers.
But what if you don’t want any of that? The Motorola Signature 27 will offer an uncharacteristic level of choice. This is the first Moto phone covered under its partnership with GrapheneOS. This privacy-focused OS is built on Android, but it doesn’t have Google apps or any of the tracking that comes with it.
Credit:
                                      Motorola Credit:

          
          Motorola
Motorola does not intend to ship a version of the Signature 27 with GrapheneOS preloaded, so it’ll be up to buyers to install it. Details on that process will come at a later date, but it should be similar to Pixel phones—unlock the bootloader, flash the software, and enjoy.
Some months back, the Graphene team revealed the first device in its Moto collaboration would be priced above Pixels , and that certainly checks out. Motorola is asking $1,599.99 for the Signature 27, putting it above even the high-end flagship phones from Samsung and Apple. It’s also within $300 dollars of foldable phones like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Motorola’s own Razr Fold (both $1,900 MSRP). Even the iPhone Duo is only $400 more than Moto’s new flagship slab.
Moto hasn’t announced any carrier partnerships yet. So you’ll have to buy the device directly from Motorola, Best Buy, or Amazon when it goes on sale November 26. Preorders will be available starting November 19 if you are so inclined.

Democratic victories and opposition to AI infrastructure highlight concerns over power bills, water use and the impact on local communities
Strong voter backlash in the US midterm elections against AI infrastructure projects, including data centres, indicates that framing the domestic buildout as key to competing with China failed to convince Americans and underscores the need to address local concerns, according to analysts.
“The argument that we need to build more data centres to win in AI against China no longer seems to have the kind of resonance it did before, if it ever did, frankly,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Centre.
Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, echoed that assessment, saying: “The lesson is that invoking China as a justification for tech and industrial investment is becoming less effective.”

China’s Yutong Bus, the world’s largest electric bus manufacturer, is seeing its overseas shipments climb steadily, with demand growing rapidly in countries such as Australia, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia and Morocco.
Based in Zhengzhou in central China’s Henan province, the company now generates more than half of its total revenue from overseas sales. New-energy models – comprising pure-electric and hybrid vehicles – have made up 25 per cent of its bus exports so far this year, a sharp increase from just 3 per cent in 2018.
Yutong holds more than 10 per cent of the global market, including China, for large and medium-sized buses and coaches, according to the company. Its competitors include domestic peers BYD, Zhongtong Bus and Xiamen King Long United Automotive Industry, as well as overseas companies like Mercedes-Benz and Volvo.

articles.title_orig: Iran Update, November 4, 2026
articles.title_zh: Iran Update, November 4, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute are publishing updates Monday through Friday to provide analysis on the war with Iran and the broader Middle East. Weekday updates cover events from the past 24-hour period, whereas weekend updates are abbreviated and cover the Houthi-Saudi conflict and major breaking developments related to the war with Iran.
Iranian leaders view the US midterm election results from November 3 as evidence that Iran’s military strategy imposed political costs on the sitting US administration. These leaders do not believe that the elections will lead to any fundamental shift in the US approach to Iran. Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a November 4 statement that Iran’s actions in the Strait of Hormuz and against US military bases demonstrated US weakness and the success of Iran’s resistance.[1] Mojtaba also warned that changes in US political leadership would not alter Washington’s approach toward Iran and that even a “slight tendency” toward surrender would only encourage further US “audacity.”[2] Mojtaba’s remarks suggest that Iran will maintain its maximalist demands regardless of the US election results, which senior Iranian officials have portrayed as evidence of the success of Iran’s strategy. Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) Secretary Major General Mohsen Rezaei separately said on November 4 that Iran had inflicted a “political defeat.”[3] Parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf also said on November 4 that American voters had rejected the war due to concerns about morality or the cost of living.[4] The beliefs of these senior leaders suggest that Iran will maintain its maximalist demands because Iranian leaders do not expect changes in US political leadership to alter Washington’s approach toward Iran. Iranian leaders therefore likely believe that Iran must secure its gains regardless of the result of the midterms.
Iran is using suboptimal systems to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. US military overmatch is currently preventing Iran from significantly decreasing the transit of civilian tankers through the Strait, however. Iran has begun to use unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs), rocket-propelled grenades (RPGs), and limpet mines to attack ships in recent weeks, according to the Wall Street Journal ( WSJ ). All these systems are suboptimal relative to the comparatively advanced anti-ship ballistic and cruise missiles and drones Iran used earlier in the conflict. Limpet mines must be attached to a ship by a person approaching the vessel, RPGs will do only limited damage to a large vessel’s hull and lack range, and known Iranian UUV capabilities presently lack the scale and sophistication required to be an optimal way to disrupt shipping. Iran’s ability to sense shipping is also suboptimal compared to coastal radars Iran used at the start of the conflict. Iranian military personnel on small craft are observing and relaying back the position of vessels, which is far less effective than coastal radar or other sensors if the target is moving.[5] Iran’s reliance on these suboptimal systems will only persist as long as the US military is present, however. Iran could acquire new radars, for example, if US aircraft stopped destroying them.
Iran may develop its UUVs into a more effective system if given time. UUVs are technically complex due to the requirement to control the system underwater at long range.[6] Iran’s current UUV platforms — at least as of 2022 — use a combination of rudimentary guidance systems and torpedo designs with slower, longer-range specifications meant primarily for anchored targets.[7] Iranian naval forces may have since adapted their UUVs to better hit moving targets. Iran presumably would have used UUVs earlier in the conflict if they were an optimal way to disrupt shipping.
ISW-CTP and Western media have observed an uptick in attacks on ships in the strait over the past month, which is consistent with ISW-CTP’s assessment that Iran may have partially reconstituted certain capabilities or is experimenting with new methods to retain a credible threat in the strait.[8] US military efforts have nonetheless been successful in escorting ships carrying oil through the strait. US Central Command (CENTCOM) Commander Admiral Brad Cooper stated on October 30 that US forces have escorted over 3,000 commercial vessels through the strait and have facilitated the transit of approximately 1.5 billion barrels of oil since this summer, for example.[9] WSJ similarly reported on October 29 that US efforts in recent weeks have enabled oil exports in the Gulf to surpass prewar levels.[10]
It is likely that Iran will invest in its unmanned capabilities in the long term, as it seeks to rebuild its naval capabilities to threaten shipping in the strait given the limitations of its conventional naval capabilities against the United States. The combined US-Israeli force repeatedly struck conventional Iranian naval vessels, effectively sinking the entirety of Iran’s surface fleet by March 11.[11] Persistent US strikes have also largely suppressed missile and drone attacks, as suggested by Iran’s reliance on these suboptimal systems. ISW-CTP assessed in March that all future attempts by the Iranian navy to blockade the Strait of Hormuz will likely employ unconventional forces such as small boats, unmanned surface vessels (USVs), and UUVs.[12] Iran may also seek to develop, expand, and diversify its use of space, air, surface, and sub-sea sensors to improve its ability to detect and fix vessels. Iran would also likely replace its current suboptimal manned spotting capabilities with more accurate autonomous sensors where possible long term. It could also use human spotters hidden among fishing vessels in the Strait of Hormuz to tip and cue more bespoke sensors in the future.
Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) and Lebanese Hezbollah advisers are reportedly stationed within Yemen to advise the Houthis on various military efforts and capabilities that primarily serve Iran’s strategic objectives.[13] The Yemeni Interior Ministry announced on November 3 that 14 IRGC officers and seven Hezbollah officials are currently deployed as advisers across Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen.[14] These advisers notably include IRGC Quds Force Brigadier General Abdolreza Shahlai, who is a long-serving emissary to the Houthis and is responsible for the deaths of US servicemembers in Iraq. [15] Shahlai is one of several senior IRGC and Hezbollah officials stationed in Sanaa, the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital, and is responsible for Houthi coordination with Iran and other Axis of Resistance groups.[16] Iran is supporting the Houthi campaign in part because Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia affect the global energy markets and increase the economic and political pressure on the United States to end the war against Iran.[17]
Most of the identified IRGC and Hezbollah advisers who are currently stationed in Yemen belong to one of three main advisory subject areas that correspond to Iranian objectives.[18] Shahlai and a diplomacy-focused adviser, Ali Mohammad Ramazani, likely advise the Houthis at the strategic level and liaise with the IRGC.[19] Many other officials are based in Hudaydah and focus on developing Houthi submersible and surface naval drones, maritime surveillance, and other naval capabilities.[20] These advisers are improving Houthi technical capabilities to attack shipping both now and in the future, and Iran surely hopes that the Houthis can support Iranian efforts to disrupt shipping in the Red Sea in future conflicts. The Iranian regime is currently using unmanned systems like UUVs and USVs to attack commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz (see above). articles.title_orig: Altar Stone mystery continues as theory overturned
articles.title_zh: Altar Stone mystery continues as theory overturned
articles.content_orig:
A new study exploring the origins of the six tonne Altar Stone at Stonehenge has ruled out a theory that it came from an area of Scotland.
The 4.9 metre sandstone slab within the circle was initially believed to have originated in Wales until a more recent study pointed towards it coming from north east Scotland.
Scientific tests were carried out in the Orcadian Basin area of Scotland, but researchers failed to find a location with the same characteristics of the stone in that area.
However study lead, Professor Duncan Pirrie from the University of South Wales, said the latest investigation has left them "far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer."
Pirrie said his latest publication on the Altar Stone has "built the clearest picture yet" and was "the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken".
Professor Nick Pearce from Aberystwyth University, who worked on the previous research, said "ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones".
The geochemistry expert said: "Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated.
"The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago."
The world-famous Wiltshire monument was constructed in multiple phases over thousands of years, between 3000 and 1600 BC. However, not all stones come from the area.
The smaller bluestones travelled around 225km from west Wales with research suggesting a few were taken directly from another circle.
The latest study combined new observations and looked at fragments of the stone in museum collections, examining structure, minerals and composition.
It has been published in the Journal of the Geological Society.

articles.title_orig: Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger found dead in Berlin hotel
articles.title_zh: Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger found dead in Berlin hotel
articles.content_orig:
Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger was found dead in a hotel in Berlin on Wednesday, the German capital's public prosecutor's office said.
Aiwanger was Bavaria's deputy premier, economy minister and the chairman of the right-wing populist Free Voters party. He was 55 years old.
The circumstances surrounding Aiwanger's death are still unclear. Police and prosecutors in the German capital have launched an investigation.
On Wednesday evening, investigators said the goal is to "determine the specific cause of death and the circumstances surrounding it, as well as to rule out any possible foul play."
Aiwanger had been feeling unwell on Wednesday, German tabloid Bild reported.
He was scheduled to deliver a speech at the opening of a party office in Berlin but canceled his appearance for health reasons, German news agency dpa reported.
Aiwanger's body was found on Wednesday evening at the "Neuer Fritz" Hotel on Friedrichstrasse in Berlin-Mitte, according to Bild .
Bavarian state premier, the Christian Social Union 's Markus Söder, has said he is "deeply shocked" by the news of his deputy's death.
"The sudden death of Hubert Aiwanger is an absolute tragedy," Söder said in a post on X.
"Our thoughts are now first and foremost with his family and his children. We mourn with them and pray for them."
Born in Lower Bavaria in southern Germany , Aiwanger was elected to the Bavarian State Parliament in 2008 with the Free Voters and became their parliamentary group leader.
Since 2018, his party has been in a coalition with the center-right CSU, the Bavarian sister party of the ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU) . Aiwanger served as the state's Minister of Economic Affairs and deputy premier.
Aiwanger was the face of the Free Voters in Bavaria and across Germany, and was known for his combative approach.
But his political success in the state did not translate to the national level, as the Free Voters never won enough seats to enter the Bundestag , Germany's federal parliament.
In the weeks before state elections in 2023, Aiwanger became embroiled in a national scandal when the Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that he had written an antisemitic leaflet during high school in the 1980s, which included references to Nazi-era atrocities such as Auschwitz.
He is survived by two children. He was not married but lived with Tanja Schweiger, a district administrator for the Free Voters.

articles.title_orig: How India Can Manage Chinese Surpluses
articles.title_zh: How India Can Manage Chinese Surpluses
articles.content_orig:
By Thomas Asplund-Meineckem , William B. Smith, and  Shiro Armstrong
China’s resurgent trade surplus has revived fears across developing Asia that it is pulling up the ladder of export-led industrialization behind it. In New Delhi, India’s bilateral trade deficit with China — over $112 billion in 2025–26 — is being read as the result of unfair Chinese competition and domestic structural weakness, both cited as grounds for protection. But viewing China primarily as a competitor misses its potentially complementary role and the case for managing the relationship rather than retreating from it.
Concerns over a ‘China squeeze’ hold that China has industrialized without ceding labor-intensive industries, partly due to its industrial policies and structurally undervalued renminbi. The argument goes that Chinese goods undercut developing countries’ firms at home and outcompete them in third markets, while China demands few of their exports, leaving developing countries little room to industrialize.
New Delhi has been especially receptive to this argument, framing economic engagement with China as a threat to be contained. In thinly veiled comments directed at China in June 2026, Minister of External Affairs Subrahmanyam Jaishankar argued that ‘the right to industrialize, indeed the capacity to do so, is being denied’ to many developing countries.
Convinced that its firms cannot compete with China on fair terms, New Delhi has turned its trade policy inwards . India has increased tariffs since 2018 to an average of around 17.6 percent, among the highest in Asia, and raised non-tariff barriers. In November 2019, India also walked out of Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) negotiations, largely over concerns it would expose Indian firms and farmers to a surge of cheap Chinese imports. But this ‘ RCEP minus China ’ strategy leaves India outside the regional production networks deeply integrated with China.
Underlying this strategy is concern about India’s bilateral trade deficit. But economies tend to run deficits with countries that supply their inputs and surpluses with those that buy their outputs. Imports of this kind reflect complementarities between economies, and by lowering costs, make local firms more productive and competitive.
China is above all a supplier to Indian manufacturing. Capital goods, machinery and intermediate goods accounted for around 87 percent of Indian imports from China in 2024.
India’s pharmaceutical and electronics industries show the value of integration into Chinese value chains. Between 2015 and 2022, Indian value added in electronics exports nearly tripled as their Chinese content rose sixfold. In pharmaceuticals, it rose by half as Chinese content doubled.
Labor-intensive industries like textiles show a similar pattern. With China moving upstream out of garment assembly, Bangladesh and Vietnam have taken substantial market share. But India’s share of global textile exports has remained stagnant at around 3 percent , with its garment makers paying higher duties on imported fabric.
Tariff and non-tariff barriers to Chinese inputs shelter upstream firms but raise costs for downstream exporters who compete with Chinese exports in foreign markets regardless. Input tariff neutrality would help Indian firms integrate into global value chains, raising domestic value added in absolute terms even if the foreign value-added share of exports rises.
Deeper integration would also help India sell more to China. Despite supplying almost 17 percent of India’s imports in 2025–26, China bought only 4.4 percent of India’s exports. Part of the gap reflects Chinese barriers in key Indian sectors, but Indian firms also struggle to match Chinese rivals on cost and scale.
Indian protectionism against China will not resolve the distortions imposed by Chinese overcapacity . At best, India’s barriers offset some of their effects — but raise costs for Indian firms. India can gain more from importing cheaper Chinese equipment, green technology and productive capacity for its own industrialization — especially given unilateral action will not change the policies driving China’s surpluses.
Genuine Chinese distortions demand a collective response through international and regional agreements. RCEP’s joint committees and ministerial meetings allow members to press Beijing on unfair practices, and its standards and customs chapters provide channels to raise the approval delays preventing Indian goods from reaching Chinese markets.
Membership would also pull India into regional production networks. RCEP’s common rules of origin make it easier to spread production across member economies, since inputs from any member count towards origin, qualifying the final good for preferential tariffs across the bloc. RCEP also provides safeguards against damaging import surges, allowing members to suspend tariff cuts or raise duties when imports injure domestic industries.
RCEP members remain open to India’s accession — New Delhi could take up an observer seat now and apply to join without the waiting period other applicants face. The agreement’s first General Review in 2027 offers a natural moment to negotiate entry.
The Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) offers further avenues for managing Chinese surpluses. China’s application to join — pending since September 2021 — offers the region leverage, holding out access to CPTPP markets in return for reform of state-owned enterprises, investment and government procurement.
The same logic applies to India, for which CPTPP membership is a longer-term goal. Its regulatory disciplines would demand reforms India’s political economy has long resisted. A staged process — beginning with a gap analysis and cooperation in less contentious areas before negotiating transition periods and carve-outs for sensitive sectors — would give policymakers time to build domestic support for reform.
Indian policymakers should understand China not only as a competitor but as a potential complementor. The trade deficit driving India inwards largely consists of inputs that make its firms more productive and competitive. Unilateral protection and absence from RCEP and CPTPP leave India outside the production networks that would allow its manufacturing sector to prosper, and without a voice to press genuine concerns. Managing the relationship through regional arrangements offers a surer way up the ladder of export-led industrialization than going it alone.

articles.title_orig: Russia, China may be more aggressive if they feel Trump is on "his way out": Brookings
articles.title_zh: Russia, China may be more aggressive if they feel Trump is on "his way out": Brookings
articles.content_orig:
Russia and China could become more aggressive over the next two years if they conclude that President Donald Trump is politically weakened and on "his way out" after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC.
Speaking on " Squawk Box Asia ," Kagan said the war with Iran had also exposed how Washington has "proved itself rather incapable militarily" in terms of capacity, which would be critical in Asia.
"Everybody can see how much our stocks are depleted in terms of interceptors and missiles, which are of vital interest in the Asian theater," he said.
Congressional Budget Office reports have estimated that the conflict depleted as much as two-thirds of U.S. missile-defense interceptors since June 2025, largely because of efforts to defend Israel against Iranian attacks. This could leave the U.S. with constrained inventories for several years.
Kagan said the deployment of three U.S. aircraft carriers to the Middle East had reduced the U.S. naval presence available in Asia, potentially giving China more room to act assertively in the region.
"I think Trump's only interest right now is in cutting economic deals with China. I don't think he has any real interest in confronting China, but that is going to lead China to be even more aggressive," he said.
In December, Trump approved an $11 billion arms package for Taiwan, but later held back on a second package worth about $14 billion, calling it a "bargaining chip" in talks with China.
China claims self-governing Taiwan as its territory. While Washington does not have a mutual defense treaty with the island, U.S. law requires it to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself.
Former CIA Director William Burns said in 2023 that Chinese President Xi Jinping had instructed the military to be ready to invade Taiwan by 2027, while stressing that this did not mean Xi had decided to launch an invasion that year or at all.
Kagan's comments come as U.S., China and Russia discuss a possible trilateral summit between Trump, Xi and President Vladimir Putin at the APEC Leaders' meeting in Shenzhen later this month.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Wednesday that Beijing was "in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state," although no agenda has been announced.
Putin had reportedly floated the idea of a three-way summit with Trump and Xi in October to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
"If it's clear that Donald Trump is on his way out, and the United States may be returning to something like normal, I don't want to overstate that, but they may feel both of them, both Russia and China, may feel that the time to move is in the next two years," Kagan said.

articles.title_orig: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
articles.title_zh: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
articles.content_orig:
Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification
The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.
MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.
“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.
“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”
It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.
China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.
The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.
MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.
The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.
But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025 , a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.
Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.
The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.
Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.
However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.
after newsletter promotion
The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.
The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.
“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.
The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.
As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.
“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.
A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships. “Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Jumps 1,500 Points On Democratic Sweep of Congress — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Jumps 1,500 Points On Democratic Sweep of Congress — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared nearly 1,600 points, or 3%, on Wednesday, its biggest gain of the year, as investors digested the impact of the Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm congressional elections.
Other indexes also jumped, with the broader S&P 500 climbing 120 points, or 1.6%, to close at 7,689 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index gaining 1.4%.
"Investors are happy to have the midterms out of the way," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, told investors in a report. "This was a major source of uncertainty, and putting it in the rear-view mirror removes a key obstacle heading into a very favorable time of year seasonally."
The shifting political winds could affect a range of issues that influence investment returns, from the pace of the data center buildout and cryptocurrency industry regulation to proposals to cap credit card interest rates.
At the same time, Wall Street analysts do not expect the outcome to derail a stock market being driven more by robust corporate profits and solid economic growth than by politics.
"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown of Capital Economics said in a note to investors.
Stocks of solar power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans.
Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Mr. Trump's social media company, the artificial intelligence sector and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. Trump Media & Technology's stock price fell nearly 25% on Wednesday, while shares of Musk-owned SpaceX and Tesla sank 3.8% and 3.3%, respectively.
Investors also expect the election results to heighten gridlock in Congress, with Democratic lawmakers now in control of both the House and Senate, and Mr. Trump threatening to wield his veto power to block any legislation he opposes.
Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to Wall Street analysts.
Meanwhile, stocks have generally performed well following midterm elections. The S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 15.5% in the six months after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970, according to figures from investment firm Edward Jones.
"Economic growth, inflation, interest rates and corporate earnings have historically mattered more to broad investment performance than the party composition of Congress, especially if the president and congressional leadership come from different parties," analysts with the Wells Fargo Investment Institute said in a report.
"We do not expect sweeping policy changes," they added. "More likely, in our view, is a split-government alignment on affordability, energy policy and opportunities from artificial intelligence."
Beyond the Beltway, the midterm electoral results could affect key issues for investors, such as the pace of data center construction, with enormous spending on artificial intelligence helping drive stocks to record highs this year while also raising concerns about a bubble in tech stocks .
"In divided government, the policy implications at the federal level may be limited, but data center policy decisions sit at the state and utility-commission level, making gubernatorial and utility races important alongside Congress, particularly Governor Abbott's loss in Texas," Jeff Buchbinder of LPL Research told investors.
"LPL Research continues to expect the buildout to occur, but strong performances by Democrats in key data center states (and pushback from the 'not in my backyard' folks) may slow it down some, potentially increasing regulatory pressure on AI infrastructure stocks including semiconductors, machinery and power generation," he added.

articles.title_orig: 3M strikes $7B settlement in ‘forever chemical’ firefighting foam cases
articles.title_zh: 3M strikes $7B settlement in ‘forever chemical’ firefighting foam cases
articles.content_orig:
3M has agreed to pay up to $7.35 billion to settle lawsuits over groundwater contamination from potentially harmful chemicals in firefighting foam and other products
Chemical manufacturer 3M will pay up to $7.35 billion to settle lawsuits by people who say they were sickened by groundwater contamination from compounds used in firefighting foam and other consumer products.
The St. Paul, Minnesota-based company announced the settlement Tuesday. It will pay the money over nine years to as many as 120,000 people who say they were harmed by exposure to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, known collectively as PFAS . The chemicals contaminated groundwater near military bases, airports and other locations where the foam was used to extinguish fires.
3M did not admit liability for the contamination under the agreement.
Called “forever chemicals” because they don’t degrade naturally in the environment, PFAS have been linked to health problems including liver and immune system damage and some cancers. The chemicals are also used in nonstick, water- and grease-resistant products, including clothing and cookware.
3M chairman William Brown called the settlement a “significant milestone” that substantially reduces uncertainty from the litigation. The company previously reached settlements in other PFAS-related lawsuits, including a $450 million agreement with the state of New Jersey to settle claims of natural resource contamination and a deal to pay more than $10 billion to many U.S. public drinking water systems .
Other manufacturers, including DuPont de Nemours Inc. and spinoffs Chemours Co. and Corteva Inc., have agreed to settlements totaling more than $1 billion to resolve PFAS claims.
Fred Thompson, an attorney with the Motley Rice law firm that helped negotiate the 3M settlement for the plaintiffs, called it welcome news for “the thousands of victims who have sought answers and accountability for nearly a decade.”
He said in a news release that the plaintiffs urgently need help covering mounting medical bills and other costs.
Under the terms of the settlement, the payouts will begin with $50 million this year, followed by yearly payments of more than $1 billion each year from 2028 to 2033.
3M could make additional payments if enough plaintiffs participate. If too few sign on, 3M has the option to cancel the settlement and continue fighting the lawsuit.
Environmental activists say PFAS manufacturers knew about the chemicals' health risks long before they became public. They noted that the same attributes that make the chemicals so valuable in many uses — resistance to breakdown — also make them hazardous to people.
The Environmental Protection Agency has set strict limits on PFAS in drinking water from public utilities and requires testing, but those rules do not apply to private wells .
A study that would help federal regulators understand which industries dump the forever chemicals with their wastewater has been stalled for two years, awaiting review by the White House Office of Management and Budget.
___ Boone reported from Boise, Idaho.

articles.title_orig: CVS to break up $117 billion business, separating pharmacies from insurance; shares fall
articles.title_zh: CVS to break up $117 billion business, separating pharmacies from insurance; shares fall
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health said Wednesday it is splitting into two companies, marking one of the largest shakeups in the healthcare industry. It’s a major reversal of the mergers that brought together the nation’s largest drugstore retailer along with health insurance giant Aetna and pharmacy benefit manager Caremark.
One company, which would house CVS’s 9,000 retail pharmacies, mail order pharmacy, specialty drug business and MinuteClinic, will be named CVS Pharmacy.
The other, comprising of Aetna, Caremark and two companies that CVS acquired that provide primary care and in-home health evaluations to senior citizens, will be called CVS Health in the interim.
The separation is expected to close in early 2028.
The breakup unwinds a strategy that began in 2007, when CVS merged with Caremark, which handles prescription benefits available to people with health insurance. In 2018, CVS acquired Aetna for $69 billion.
“We’re basically taking what I believe is one great company and making it two,” said CVS CEO David Joyner in a statement Wednesday.
The company split will have little impact on the way people shop at CVS – the company didn’t announce any closures as part of the news – nor will affect what patients pay for prescriptions.
Pharmacy benefit management businesses work on the backend, negotiating directly with drugmakers on the cost of prescription drugs. But CVS’s drugstores and Caremark insurance operate separately. Splitting into two companies won’t change how they function.
The split does, however, mark a major step back from the widespread trend to integrate various parts of the healthcare industry – including insurers, pharmacy benefit managers and providers – into massive conglomerates. That consolidation has come under attack from consumer advocates and state and federal lawmakers for wielding too much control of the sector, leading to higher costs for patients. Some members of Congress have called for breaking up the companies.
Also, health insurers have come under cost pressure because Americans are using more healthcare services. Meanwhile, lawmakers and regulators are seeking to reform the pharmacy benefit manager industry just as it contends with new players looking to chip away at the dominance of Caremark and other major PBMs.
Meanwhile, CVS’ retail business has been hampered by consumers shifting to online channels, where the company still lags leaders like Amazon, Michael Cherny, an analyst with Leerink Partners, wrote in a client note on Tuesday evening after reports of the split surfaced.
Cherny, who called the news “a complete shock,” wrote that CVS’ pharmacy business has been performing well so “perhaps the outlook for a standalone retail pharmacy (still with meaningful scale and leverage on its own) is stronger now than before.”
Joyner, who will lead the new CVS Health company, took over as CEO in 2024 in the wake of layoffs, store closings and poor stock performance.
Shares of CVS Health, which have risen since Joyner’s appointment, fell 12% in midday trading after initially ticking up in premarket trading. Shareholders will get shares of both companies in a tax-free transaction, according to the company.
CVS also reported higher third-quarter earnings and revenue Wednesday, due primarily to better results from its Health Care Benefits segment. The company also raised its earnings guidance for the rest of this year.
CVS has 9,000 locations across the United States, 800 of which operate “MinuteClinics” staffed by nurse practitioners and physician assistants. It has 30,000 pharmacists and 200,000 employees in its stores, the company said during an earnings call Wednesday.
